paragraphs.text: 4.2. What the responsibility includes
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: What the responsibility includes

paragraphs.text: The responsibility of the parties to manage their dispute and to plan its resolution requires the parties (a) to act in a manner that furthers the purpose and intention of these rules described in rule 1.2, (b) in an action categorized as a standard case, to respond in a substantive way and within a reasonable time to any proposal for the conduct of an action, (c) in an action categorized as a complex case, to meet or to adjust dates in a timely way in a complex case litigation plan, (d) when the complexity or the nature of an action requires it, to apply to the Court for direction, or request case management under rule 4.12, and (e) to consider and engage in one or more dispute resolution processes described in rule 4.16(1) unless the Court waives that requirement.

paragraphs.text: 4.3. Categories of court action
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Categories of court action

paragraphs.text: (1) For the purpose of these rules, actions are categorized as (a) standard cases, or (b) complex cases. (2) In deciding whether an action should be categorized as a standard or complex case, the parties or the Court, as the case requires, must consider the following factors: (a) the amount of the claim, the number and nature of the claims, and the complexity of the action; (b) the number of parties; (c) the number of documents involved; (d) the number and complexity of issues and how important they are; (e) how long questioning under Part 5 is likely to take; (f) whether expert reports will be required and, if so, the time it will take to exchange reports and to question experts under Part 5; (g) whether medical examinations and reports under Part 5, Division 3 will be required; (h) any other matter that should be considered to meet the purpose and intention of the rules described in rule 1.2; (i) whether a third party claim has been or is likely to be made. (3) If, within 4 months after the date a statement of defence is filed, the parties do not agree on whether the action is a standard or complex case, and the Court does not otherwise order, the action is to be categorized as a standard case.

paragraphs.text: 4.4. Standard case obligations
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Standard case obligations

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless the parties otherwise agree, or the Court otherwise orders, and subject to matters arising beyond the control of the parties, the parties to an action categorized as a standard case must, within a reasonable time considering the nature of the action, complete each of the following steps or stages in the action: (a) close of pleadings; (b) disclosure of information under Part 5; (c) at least one of the dispute resolution processes described in rule 4.16(1), unless the requirement is waived by the Court; (d) application for a trial date. (2) A party to an action categorized as a standard case may serve on the other party a proposed litigation plan or a proposal for the completion or timing of any stage or step in the action, and if no agreement is reached, any party may apply to the Court for a procedural or other order respecting the plan or proposal.

paragraphs.text: 4.5. Complex case obligations
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Complex case obligations

paragraphs.text: (1) The parties to an action categorized as a complex case must, within 4 months after the date that the parties agree to the categorization or the Court determines that the action is a complex case, (a) agree on a complex case litigation plan, and (b) unless reasons are given in the plan not to do so, (i) establish a date by which the real issues in dispute will be identified, (ii) agree on a protocol for the organization and production of records, (iii) set a date by which disclosure of records will be completed under rule 5.5, (iv) set a date by which questioning under Part 5 will be completed, (v) set a date by which all experts' reports and rebuttal and surrebuttal expert reports will be served, (vi) set a date by which reports of any health care professionals will be obtained, and (vii) agree on an estimated date to apply for a trial date. (2) When a complex case litigation plan or an amendment to the plan is agreed to, the plaintiff must file it and serve it on all parties.

paragraphs.text: 4.10. Assistance by the Court
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Assistance by the Court

paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may, at any time, direct the parties and any other person to attend a conference with the Court. (2) The participants in the conference may consider (a) dispute resolution possibilities, the process for them, and how they can be facilitated; (b) simplification or clarification of a claim, a pleading, a question, an issue, an application or a proceeding; (c) a complex case litigation plan or a modification to the plan; (d) case management by a judge; (e) practice, procedural or other issues or questions and how to resolve them; (f) any other matter that may aid in the resolution or facilitate the resolution of a claim, application or proceeding or otherwise meet the purpose and intention of these rules described in rule 1.2. (3) If a party files an application for a conference under this rule, that party must (a) give a reason for the conference, and (b) file and serve on every other party notice of the application and any material to be relied on in support of the application a reasonable time before the date the conference is scheduled to take place. (4) The Court may make a procedural order before, at or following the conference.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.10:1 Rule 4.10 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.10. Pre-trial Conference Negotiations Are Privileged Settlements are within the scope of a pretrial conference: rule 219(1)(d). However, a pretrial conference judge cannot order an agreement; the most such a judge might do would be to recognize an agreement which the parties have made between themselves by recording it, or signing a consent order. If the settlement discussions do not result in a formal order or settlement, I am of the view that they remain mere negotiations and, therefore, privileged. In summary on this point, a pretrial conference may address the possibilities of settlement. If a formal settlement is not executed, the pretrial conference judge may hear the trial. However, if a formal settlement is not reached, discussions relating to settlement are privileged; if recorded by any party or the pretrial conference judge (for example with a view to post-trial cost submissions), the report of negotiations must be filed separately from the main file, in a closed file analogous to files kept under Part 12 of the Rules—Compromise using Court Process. Perepelecta v. Perepelecta (1990), 103 A.R. 236 (Q.B.), at 238, per Veit J.

paragraphs.text: 4.11. Ways the Court may manage action
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Ways the Court may manage action

paragraphs.text: The Court may manage an action in one or more of the following ways, in which case the responsibility of the parties to manage their dispute is modified accordingly: (a) the Court may make a procedural order; (b) the Court may direct a conference under rule 4.10; (c) on request under rule 4.12, or on the initiative of the Chief Justice under rule 4.13, the Chief Justice may appoint a case management judge for the action; (d) the Court may make an order under a rule providing for specific direction or a remedy.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.11:1 Rule 4.11 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.11. 1. Standard of Review Thus, the reasonableness standard has been described in the jurisprudence in a variety of different terms. Regardless of the variation in terminology found in the case law, the standard of review applicable to the exercise of discretion by a case management judge is no different than that for any discretionary decision made in chambers; that standard, simply put, is one of “reasonableness”. Indian Residential Schools, Re (2001), 96 Alta. L.R. (3d) 16 (C.A.) at 23, per curiam. 2. Failure to Comply with Directions In 291617 Alberta Ltd. v. Kretschmer (1997), 193 A.R. 180 (C.A.), the appellants appealed an order directing portions of the costs awarded against them to be paid on a solicitor-client basis. In the course of judgment, the Court of Appeal commented on the possible consequences of thwarting the pre-trial conference process. At pp. 185-87 the court said: The main pretrial conference process became abortive because the appellants declined to give their counsel any authority to agree to anything. They did not insist on their draft of agreed facts and documents; they declined to agree to any facts or exhibits, or even to negotiate any more. The material entered by agreement for appeal confirms that several ways. That refusal to negotiate had two consequences. First, all the months of pretrial conferences before then became largely a waste of everyone's time, not least the pretrial conference judge's. Second, the trial then became longer than it would have been had there been some agreement about issues, facts, and exhibits. The trial judge had ample opportunity to see the results of that firsthand. We understand that it took ten days to put in the oral evidence. One hundred and forty separate exhibits were marked. The first 73 were marked on the first 7 pages of transcript; they were put in bulk. But the other 67 were marked at intervals over the course of the trial. A lot of them are letters and contemporary documents whose identity and authenticity could not have been in any serious question. There were no agreed facts. There were about 36 pages of opening statements, and the first live witness did not take the stand until after the first mid-morning break. Rules 190, 230, and 219 exist precisely to prevent such horse-and-buggy proceedings. (Not to mention a number of Queen's Bench Practice Directions.) Counsel for the appellants objects that they do not have to agree to anything, and have a right to make the plaintiffs prove their case. Indeed they do have that right. But once it is found who wins the suit, rule 601 also gives the trial judge a very wide power to decide who shall pay for making the plaintiff prove everything, and on what scale. One fetter on that power is rule 230(4), which says that the costs of proving what should have been admitted must be paid by the party who failed to admit (unless the failure was reasonable). It is probable that that applies directly to proceedings under rule 219, but if it does not, then it would apply by analogy under rule 4. And so would the basic principles of costs. There is another basis for the award of costs. Rule 219(2), (3) calls for orders and directions by the pretrial conference judge, which shall govern later proceedings. There were a number of them here, given over many months. (They are reproduced in the agreed facts about costs.) It appears that the appellants ultimately decided to fly in the face of most of them. That may be contempt of court under rule 703, and solicitor-client costs are an appropriate remedy for that. Equally important is another consideration. Rule 230(4) says that the key to costs is whether the refusal to admit was reasonable. Our [modern] rules of pleading are very lax, but they are counterbalanced by a very important rule which is understood as a basic principle but rarely cited, rule 128. It reads as follows: 128. Where the court is of opinion that any allegations of facts denied or not admitted, ought to have been admitted, the court may make an order with respect to any extra costs occasioned by their having been denied or not admitted. In other words, the courts are here to try real disputes, not to play games of “Catch Me If You Can”. A different meter runs if such games are played. It appears to us that that is just what the trial judge did here. While party-party costs might be apt in some special circumstances, especially where the party unreasonably refusing to admit ultimately won the suit, none of that applies here. There is no real item in Schedule C for pretrial conferences, and a different principle applies where there is no real dispute. The trial judge after careful inquiry concluded that the pretrial conferences were a waste of everyone's time and money through the fault of the appellants. There is evidence to support that, there is no error in law or principle, and appellate courts should be slow to second-guess costs decisions. There is no free lunch. It is notorious that at the moment party-party costs cover only a small part of a party's legal bill, and none of his own expenses or lost income from delay, lost interest, or his own wasted time. To award the respondents party-party costs equalling (say) 20% of the their real wasted legal bills, would be to force the wholly innocent respondents to bear 80% of those wasted expenses. Besides, we must encourage use of the pretrial process. Often it will not work if it depends solely upon every party and every lawyer to a complex suit displaying full goodwill. It needs teeth. In the 1930s, its predecessor, the summons or motion for directions, died in England and Alberta. That occurred because solicitors would not take it seriously, and it turned into a useless perfunctory thing. There were no trial backlogs then, but there was a supply of lawyers who were willing to work for very low fees. Today, it is bad enough that litigation is necessarily slow and expensive. The public will not stomach adding more delay and expense by conduct of the sort found here. So the appeal against the costs award is also dismissed.

paragraphs.text: 4.12. Request for case management
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Request for case management

paragraphs.text: (1) A request for a case management order must be made in writing to the Chief Justice and a copy of the request must be served on each of the other parties. (2) The request must state (a) the reason for the request, and (b) whether any of the other parties agrees with the request. (3) An action commenced or continued under the Class Proceedings Act must have a case management judge appointed for the action unless the Chief Justice decides otherwise, and the request for a case management judge must be made no later than the date on which the first application in respect of the class proceeding is made under section 2(2) of the Class Proceedings Act.

sentences.text: Appointment of case management judge

paragraphs.text: The Chief Justice may order that an action be subject to case management and appoint a judge as the case management judge for the action for one or more of the following reasons: (a) to encourage the parties to participate in a dispute resolution process; (b) to promote and ensure the fair and efficient conduct and resolution of the action; (c) to keep the parties on schedule; (d) to facilitate preparation for trial and the scheduling of a trial date.

paragraphs.text: 4.14. Authority of case management judge
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Authority of case management judge

paragraphs.text: (1) A case management judge, or if the circumstances require, any other judge, may (a) order that steps be taken by the parties to identify, simplify or clarify the real issues in dispute, (b) establish, substitute or amend a complex case litigation plan and order the parties to comply with it, (c) make an order to facilitate an application, proceeding, questioning or pre-trial proceeding, (d) make an order to promote the fair and efficient resolution of the action by trial, (e) facilitate efforts the parties may be willing to take towards the efficient resolution of the action or any issue in the action through negotiation or a dispute resolution process other than trial, (f) make any procedural order that the judge considers necessary, or (g) as a case management judge, exercise the powers that a trial judge has by adjudicating any issues that can be decided before commencement of the trial, including those related to (i) the admissibility of evidence, (ii) expert witnesses, (iii) admissions, and (iv) adverse inferences. (2) Unless the Chief Justice or the case management judge otherwise directs, or these rules otherwise provide, the case management judge must hear every application filed with respect to the action for which the case management judge is appointed. (3) A decision that results from the exercise of the power referred to in subrule (1)(g) is binding on the parties for the remainder of the trial, even if the judge who hears the evidence on the merits is not the same as the case management judge, unless the court is satisfied that it would not be in the interests of justice because, among other considerations, fresh evidence has been adduced. Alta. Reg. 85/2016, s. 1(2)

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.14:1 Rule 4.14 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.11. In MTM Commercial Trust v. Statesman Riverside Quays Ltd., 2022 ABCA 328, 2022 CarswellAlta 2819, Justice Slatter made these comments about intent of case management, and the effect of case management orders: [45] For example, there is nothing that prevents the parties from expressly or implicitly isolating one issue and putting that issue before the Court for resolution, while accepting that other collateral issues will be resolved in the future: see R. 7.1; Raywalt. Further, the fact that one disputed issue in an action is put forward for resolution does not mean that the parties have abandoned any claims that every party acknowledges will have to be resolved in some future proceeding: see reasons at para. 25. [46] The rule against litigation by instalment is not fully applicable when it comes to case management decisions. Case management is in fact an institutionalized form of litigation by instalment. The concept is that a single trial judge will become immersed in the litigation, will become familiar with the facts and issues, and will be able to resolve sub-issues that arise. This creates a more productive platform for settlement discussions, and can limit the issues that must be resolved at an eventual trial. [47] The summary disposition of a narrow issue in case management should not raise an issue estoppel or res judicata on every other issue that might possibly have been brought forward at the same time. It cannot be that summary disposition of an issue is not possible in case management unless all related issues are summarily resolved at the same time. Any such rule would make the summary disposition of an issue at case management a trap, and would undermine the efficacy of the process. [48] Therefore, if the case management judge was asked to decide a discrete issue, and did decide that issue, it does not follow that every related issue is res judicata. Further, the opinion of the case management judge as to the scope of the first decision is highly relevant: Weinrich Contracting Ltd v Wiebe, 2022 ABCA 176 at para. 23; Sans Souci Limited v VRL Services Limited, [2012] UKPC 6 at para. 13. [49] Further, any resistance to “litigation by instalment”, as it applies to pre-trial proceedings, is tempered by the fact that amendments to the pleadings are possible at any time, even up to or during the trial. Just because one narrow issue has been resolved does not automatically foreclose amendments to further define the pleadings, although obviously the scope and outcome of the issue that was summarily resolved would be relevant to whether further amendments are appropriate.

paragraphs.text: 4.16. Dispute resolution processes
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Dispute resolution processes

paragraphs.text: (1) The responsibility of the parties to manage their dispute includes good faith participation in one or more of the following dispute resolution processes with respect to all or any part of the action: (a) a dispute resolution process in the private or government sectors involving an impartial third person; (b) a Court annexed dispute resolution process; (c) a judicial dispute resolution process described in rules 4.17 to 4.21; (d) any program or process designated by the Court for the purpose of this rule. (2) On application, the Court may waive the responsibility of the parties under this rule, but only if (a) before the action started the parties engaged in a dispute resolution process and the parties and the Court believe that a further dispute resolution process would not be beneficial, (b) the nature of the claim is not one, in all the circumstances, that will or is likely to result in an agreement between the parties, (c) there is a compelling reason why a dispute resolution process should not be attempted by the parties, (d) the Court is satisfied that engaging in a dispute resolution process would be futile, or (e) the claim is of such a nature that a decision by the Court is necessary or desirable. (3) The parties must attend the hearing of an application under subrule (2) unless the Court otherwise orders. (4) A case management judge or a case conference judge may, on application or on the Court's own motion, by order direct that the parties participate in a dispute resolution process. (5) In determining whether an order under subrule (4) should be made, the case management judge or case conference judge may consider all relevant circumstances, including (a) the issues in the litigation, (b) the nature of the cause of action and the relief claimed, (c) the identity, relationship and means of the parties, (d) whether the action has proceeded to a stage at which alternative dispute resolution is likely to be successful, including whether record production and questioning are sufficiently advanced to support the dispute resolution process, and (e) whether any of the factors in subrule (2) justify delaying, modifying or dispensing with the need to participate in a dispute resolution process. (6) As part of an order made under subrule (4), the case management judge or case conference judge may give directions respecting any aspect of the dispute resolution process, including (a) the identity of a neutral third party to be involved in the process, (b) where an equal sharing of the expenses is not appropriate, directions apportioning the responsibility of each party for the expenses of the neutral third party and other disbursements relating to the process, (c) the time, location, structure or conduct of the process, and (d) the consequences of the failure of any party to comply with any directions, or to pay its share of the expenses. Alta. Reg. 126/2023, s. 2

paragraphs.text: 4.16. Dispute resolution processes
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Dispute resolution processes

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.16:1 Rule 4.16 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.16. 1. General Overview (Including need to leave to appeal) In Strawson v. Strawson, 2024 ABCA 126, the parties in a “high conflict matrimonial” lawsuit involving issues about matrimonial property, debts, parenting, and support, agreed to submit their dispute to judicial dispute resolution (JDR). They agreed that the outcome would be “binding”, and they entered into an “Agreement For Binding Judicial Dispute Resolution”. The Justice who conducted the JDR ruled that $70,000 of support arrears need not be paid. The Appellant (to whom the arrears were owed) sought (1) leave to appeal the decision (without conceding that such leave was necessary), and (2) an order of the Court of Appeal setting aside the judgment which erased the $70,000 of arrears. The Court of Appeal concluded that leave to appeal was necessary because the judgment resulting from the JDR process was a consent order (paragraph 16 of the Court of Appeal’s decision). In the course of resolving the issues before it, and ultimately dismissing the appeal, the Court provided a general overview of the Judicial Dispute Resolution process. The Court said: [10] Rule 4.16 requires all parties to participate in a dispute resolution process before trial. One option is the “Judicial Dispute Resolution Process” enabled by R. 4.18. This process is unique, because it is annexed to the court adjudicative processes and involves the participation of one of the judges of the Court. Because the JDR process is annexed to other court processes, and recognized by the Rules, the JDR judge is said to be “acting in a judicial capacity”: JW Abernethy Management & Consulting Ltd v 705589 Alberta Ltd and Trillium Homes Ltd, 2005 ABCA 103 at para. 21, 44 Alta LR (4th) 24, 367 AR 38. The history of the process is outlined in that decision at paras. 7-12, 35. [11] Judicial dispute resolution is designed as a consensual process. Under R. 4.18(1)(a) all parties must agree to participate, and generally the outcome of the JDR arises from the consensual agreement of the parties to settle the dispute. The Rules do not specifically anticipate a “binding JDR”, although such sessions have become common. Some litigants are not prepared to invest the resources required to properly conduct a JDR without assurance that a final resolution will result. Many parties sensibly view dispute resolution in this way as an economical, efficient, expeditious, and fair method of finally resolving their disputes. The participation of a judge of the Court enhances the credibility of the process. [12] JDR sessions are confidential and without prejudice: Adeshina v Litwiniuk & Co, 2010 ABQB 80 at paras. 132-38, 483 AR 81, 24 Alta LR (5th) 67. If the parties fail to reach agreement, what is said or conceded during the session is covered by the settlement privilege. That does not prevent examination of whether a settlement was reached, or determination of the exact terms of the settlement: Bellatrix Exploration Ltd v Penn West Petroleum Ltd, 2013 ABCA 10 at para. 29, 542 AR 83, 81 Alta LR (5th) 84. However, the record available is limited by R. 4.19. If agreement is not reached at the JDR, R. 4.21 provides that the JDR judge must not, without consent, be involved in any subsequent application or trial of the action. [13] The opinion of the JDR judge in a binding JDR is not an adjudication of the dispute in the technical sense. The binding JDR judge derives his or her authority from the binding JDR agreement entered into by the parties. As the Agreement specifically acknowledges, the JDR judge was not bound by the rules of evidence, nor by conventional court procedures. “Judicial Dispute Resolution is not a trial process and should not be faulted for its departure from usual trial methods”: Shannon v Shannon, 2023 ABCA 79 at para. 15, 60 Alta LR (7th) 81. [14] In this case the Agreement authorized the JDR judge to sign a consent judgment incorporating his or her opinion on the fair resolution of the issues even if one of the parties objected. In Abernethy Management it was suggested at paras. 26, 30 that the outcome of a binding JDR session was a form of contract, and that it could only be enforced by a separate action on that contract. That approach would deprive the binding JDR process of much of its practical utility. Abernethy Management was decided before the JDR process was formally recognized in R. 4.18, and the concept of “binding” JDR’s was controversial: Abernethy Management at paras. 12, 37. The “binding mediation” agreement in issue there stated that the outcome of the JDR session would be “enforceable at law in the same manner as an arbitration award”. It did not authorize the binding JDR judge to sign an order implementing the outcome of the JDR session. It has been overtaken by the approach in this Agreement where the parties consent to the JDR judge signing a judgment to finalize the process. [15] One consequence of the JDR process generally, and of the binding JDR process specifically, is that there are few remedies open to a dissatisfied participant. There are no transcripts available, no sworn evidence is given, and exhibits are not formally entered and marked. Fact findings made will not necessarily be set out. Compromise is intended to drive the outcome. Thus, the usual platform for an appeal is missing. Further, the concept of a “reviewable error” in the opinion of the JDR judge is elusive, because of the wide mandate given to him or her in the binding JDR agreement. Permission to Appeal [16] The respondent is correct that an order or judgment arising from a judicial dispute resolution session is a consent order, and permission to appeal is required: Shannon at para. 23. That is more obviously the case with an order or judgment arising out of a non-binding JDR, where the order reflects a settlement. The status of the order does not change when the JDR judge has to resolve some disputes about the proper form of order to implement the settlement reached at the non-binding JDR. [17] The same is true of an order or judgment following a binding JDR process, which is also a form of consent order, and permission to appeal is required: Shannon at paras. 28-29; R. 14.5(1)(d). While the parties have not directly consented to that order or judgment, they have consented to the process under which the JDR judge signs an order or judgment: Keeder v AlGendy, 2020 ABCA 420 at paras. 15-17. As noted, clause 12 of the Agreement specifically acknowledged that “the Justice shall grant a Judgment containing the terms the Justice determines are consistent with the decision made irrespective of whether or not a party agrees with those terms”. The judgment following this binding JDR session should therefore be treated as a consent order for the purposes of R. 14.5(1)(d). [18] Clause 13 of the Agreement recites that “the Consent Judgment cannot be appealed to the Court of Appeal”. Appeal rights are strictly statutory. The parties cannot expand or reduce those rights by contract, although in some situations they could waive their right to appeal. Consent judgments cannot be appealed as of right, but they can be appealed if permission is obtained under R. 14.5(1)(d). As in this appeal, binding JDR agreements often confirm a limitation on appeal rights, which may in some cases amount to a full waiver of those appeal rights. [19] Permission will not easily be obtained to appeal a consent judgment arising from a JDR session. The premise of the JDR process is that the parties have agreed to resolving their dispute outside the normal adversarial process, and the party seeking permission will have to explain why he or she should be entitled to step around that agreement: Steenberg v Steenberg, 2023 ABCA 132 at para. 13; Laanep v Lawson, 2021 ABCA 214 at para. 3. Mere dissatisfaction with the outcome, or that a different result may have emerged following a full trial, are insufficient reasons for an appeal. The applicant will have to show some important question of law or precedent, a reasonable prospect of success, and that an appeal would not prejudice the other party: Basaraba v Tibbetts, 2021 ABCA 369 at para. 11. [20] In this appeal the requirement for permission was raised. The Case Management Officer was not able to rule whether or not permission was required because of the appellant’s argument that the order under appeal had not in fact arisen out of the JDR process, and therefore was not a consent order. By the time the application to strike and the cross-application for permission were brought, oral argument of the appeal was ready to be scheduled. As a result, a single duty judge directed that the cross-applications and the appeal itself be argued concurrently. The application to strike and the cross application for permission to appeal are, however, essentially moot and no formal adjudication of them is required. The Appeal of the Consent Judgment Procedure [21] The appellant frames her first ground of appeal as involving the JDR judge “exceeding his jurisdiction in varying his final judgment at all and in the absence of notice or an application”. By using terms such as “jurisdiction”, “absence of notice”, and “absence of an application” the appellant analogizes the JDR process to the ordinary court adjudicative process. However, while the JDR process may be annexed to the ordinary processes of the court, it is distinct. [22] A JDR judge has a wide discretion as to how to conduct the session. Subject to any agreement or understanding of the parties and the Rules on JDRs, the judge is not bound by the rules of evidence, nor is he or she obliged to follow any particular procedure. While it is expected that a certain level of procedural fairness will be observed at the JDR, the process does not assume any requirement of formal notice, nor does it require formal “applications”. [23] In this case it became apparent that the letter written by the JDR judge on November 9, 2022 was unclear. The parties appeared in docket court to outline the problem and were referred back to the JDR judge. The appearance before the JDR judge on July 12, 2023 was to resolve that ambiguity. No further notice was required, nor was there a need for a formal application. On the facts shown by this record, there was no inherent procedural unfairness involved. Finality [24] The second challenge, that the JDR judge “endorsed an order inconsistent with the judgment”, raises the question of the finality of the opinion of a binding JDR judge. Part of the allegation that the JDR judge “exceeded his jurisdiction” also relates to his clarification of the ambiguity in the November 9, 2022 letter. [25] There will undoubtedly come a point where a binding JDR judge should be regarded as having spent his or her mandate, or what would be described in a more formal context as becoming “functus”. The stage at which that occurs would depend on the circumstances, but thereafter no further variations to the binding JDR opinion are appropriate. That point was not, however, reached in this case. [26] First of all, the order of March 25, 2022 could not exhaust the JDR process, because it expressly provided in clause 16 that the parties had consented to the continuation of the process. Further information was to be provided to the JDR judge, following which he would render an opinion on the outstanding issues, including retroactive support and arrears. [27] The letter of November 9, 2022 was intended to resolve the outstanding issues, but the JDR judge agreed it contained ambiguities. In such a circumstance, it is not objectionable for the JDR judge to clarify his original intention. Even though the processes are different, it is noteworthy that until a judgment or order is actually entered, a trial judge has the ability to vary or modify it: R. 9.13. A judge presiding at a binding JDR cannot have any less flexibility than that. [28] The appellant argues that two weeks after the letter of November 9, 2022 the mandate of the binding JDR judge ended. After that point, R. 4.21 prevented him having any further involvement in the process, at least without consent. This argument is based on clause 12 of the Agreement: 12. If an Order (judgement) is not issued at the conclusion of the JDR, both parties agree that if they are unable to come to agreement on settling the minutes of the Judgment arising from the decision made by the Justice within two weeks of the conclusion of the JDR either party may apply to the Justice to finalize such terms and the Justice shall grant a Judgment containing the terms the Justice determines are consistent with the decision made irrespective of whether or not a party agrees with those terms. This clause, however, does not limit the mandate of the binding JDR judge. [29] The proper meaning of clause 12 is a matter of contractual interpretation. It should be interpreted against the background that access to judges is limited, and it often would be difficult to schedule within two weeks. On a proper interpretation, the phrase “within two weeks of the conclusion”, relates back to the phrase “unable to come to agreement on settling the minutes”. In other words, it does not limit the phrase “may apply to the Justice”. Clause 12 means if the “parties … are unable to come to agreement within two weeks of the conclusion of the JDR on settling the minutes of the Judgment” they may apply for directions. This interpretation gives the binding JDR judge the same flexibility as would be provided to a trial judge under R. 13.5. [30] The appellant argues that the JDR judge was not entitled to participate in the clarification hearing of July 12, 2023, because R. 4.21 precludes the JDR judge from involvement in any subsequent application or trial of the action. The appearance on July 12, 2023 was, however, a continuation of the JDR, and not a further application or proceeding. [31] The entry of the judgment of July 12, 2023, which is the subject of this appeal, is the most likely end to the binding JDR process. It reduced to writing the final resolution of the dispute and opinion of the JDR judge in a formal judgment of the Court. The clarifications offered by the JDR judge prior to that date do not reflect any error that can be reviewed on appeal. The JDR judge did not “endorse an order inconsistent with the judgment”, because the “judgment” (or more properly, the “opinion”) was not fixed until the clarification of July 12, 2023 and the filing of the judgment. Substance of the Decision [32] The appellant objects, in particular, to the setting aside of the approximately $70,000 of alleged arrears. The appellant argues that this outcome was inconsistent with prior interlocutory orders, and is not consistent with the amounts that would be calculated under the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines and the Child Support Guidelines. Interlocutory support orders are not final and are always subject to review at trial or when the dispute is finally settled: Durocher v Klementovich, 2013 ABCA 115 at para. 20, 544 AR 151. The Agreement did not specify that the JDR judge was not entitled to depart from the provisional amounts set in those prior orders, and indeed it is clear that the accuracy of those orders was directly in issue. Further, the parties do not agree on the factual foundation of this aspect of their dispute, precluding appellate review. [33] The mandate of the JDR judge was to bring finality to the dispute through a binding settlement. General Overview (Including need to leave to appeal) In Strawson v.

Strawson, 2024 ABCA 126, the parties in a “high conflict matrimonial” lawsuit involving issues about matrimonial property, debts, parenting, and support, agreed to submit their dispute to judicial dispute resolution (JDR).
They agreed that the outcome would be “binding”, and they entered into an “Agreement For Binding Judicial Dispute Resolution”.
The Justice who conducted the JDR ruled that $70,000 of support arrears need not be paid.

The Appellant (to whom the arrears were owed) sought (1) leave to appeal the decision (without conceding that such leave was necessary), and (2) an order of the Court of Appeal setting aside the judgment which erased the $70,000 of arrears.
The Court of Appeal concluded that leave to appeal was necessary because the judgment resulting from the JDR process was a consent order (paragraph 16 of the Court of Appeal’s decision).
In the course of resolving the issues before it, and ultimately dismissing the appeal, the Court provided a general overview of the Judicial Dispute Resolution process.
The Court said: [10] Rule 4.16 requires all parties to participate in a dispute resolution process before trial.
One option is the “Judicial Dispute Resolution Process” enabled by R.
This process is unique, because it is annexed to the court adjudicative processes and involves the participation of one of the judges of the Court.

Because the JDR process is annexed to other court processes, and recognized by the Rules, the JDR judge is said to be “acting in a judicial capacity”: JW Abernethy Management & Consulting Ltd v 705589 Alberta Ltd and Trillium Homes Ltd, 2005 ABCA 103 at para.
The history of the process is outlined in that decision at paras.
[11] Judicial dispute resolution is designed as a consensual process.
Under R.
4.18(1)(a) all parties must agree to participate, and generally the outcome of the JDR arises from the consensual agreement of the parties to settle the dispute.
The Rules do not specifically anticipate a “binding JDR”, although such sessions have become common.
Some litigants are not prepared to invest the resources required to properly conduct a JDR without assurance that a final resolution will result.
Many parties sensibly view dispute resolution in this way as an economical, efficient, expeditious, and fair method of finally resolving their disputes.
The participation of a judge of the Court enhances the credibility of the process.
[12] JDR sessions are confidential and without prejudice: Adeshina v Litwiniuk & Co, 2010 ABQB 80 at paras.
If the parties fail to reach agreement, what is said or conceded during the session is covered by the settlement privilege.

That does not prevent examination of whether a settlement was reached, or determination of the exact terms of the settlement: Bellatrix Exploration Ltd v Penn West Petroleum Ltd, 2013 ABCA 10 at para.
However, the record available is limited by R.
If agreement is not reached at the JDR, R.
4.21 provides that the JDR judge must not, without consent, be involved in any subsequent application or trial of the action.
[13] The opinion of the JDR judge in a binding JDR is not an adjudication of the dispute in the technical sense.
The binding JDR judge derives his or her authority from the binding JDR agreement entered into by the parties.

As the Agreement specifically acknowledges, the JDR judge was not bound by the rules of evidence, nor by conventional court procedures. “Judicial Dispute Resolution is not a trial process and should not be faulted for its departure from usual trial methods”: Shannon v Shannon, 2023 ABCA 79 at para.
15, 60 Alta LR (7th) 81.
[14] In this case the Agreement authorized the JDR judge to sign a consent judgment incorporating his or her opinion on the fair resolution of the issues even if one of the parties objected.
In Abernethy Management it was suggested at paras.
26, 30 that the outcome of a binding JDR session was a form of contract, and that it could only be enforced by a separate action on that contract.
That approach would deprive the binding JDR process of much of its practical utility.
Abernethy Management was decided before the JDR process was formally recognized in R.
4.18, and the concept of “binding” JDR’s was controversial: Abernethy Management at paras.
The “binding mediation” agreement in issue there stated that the outcome of the JDR session would be “enforceable at law in the same manner as an arbitration award”.
It did not authorize the binding JDR judge to sign an order implementing the outcome of the JDR session.
It has been overtaken by the approach in this Agreement where the parties consent to the JDR judge signing a judgment to finalize the process.
[15] One consequence of the JDR process generally, and of the binding JDR process specifically, is that there are few remedies open to a dissatisfied participant.
There are no transcripts available, no sworn evidence is given, and exhibits are not formally entered and marked.
Fact findings made will not necessarily be set out.
Compromise is intended to drive the outcome.
Thus, the usual platform for an appeal is missing.
Further, the concept of a “reviewable error” in the opinion of the JDR judge is elusive, because of the wide mandate given to him or her in the binding JDR agreement.

Permission to Appeal [16] The respondent is correct that an order or judgment arising from a judicial dispute resolution session is a consent order, and permission to appeal is required: Shannon at para.
That is more obviously the case with an order or judgment arising out of a non-binding JDR, where the order reflects a settlement.
The status of the order does not change when the JDR judge has to resolve some disputes about the proper form of order to implement the settlement reached at the non-binding JDR.
[17] The same is true of an order or judgment following a binding JDR process, which is also a form of consent order, and permission to appeal is required: Shannon at paras.

While the parties have not directly consented to that order or judgment, they have consented to the process under which the JDR judge signs an order or judgment: Keeder v AlGendy, 2020 ABCA 420 at paras.

As noted, clause 12 of the Agreement specifically acknowledged that “the Justice shall grant a Judgment containing the terms the Justice determines are consistent with the decision made irrespective of whether or not a party agrees with those terms”.
The judgment following this binding JDR session should therefore be treated as a consent order for the purposes of R.
[18] Clause 13 of the Agreement recites that “the Consent Judgment cannot be appealed to the Court of Appeal”.
Appeal rights are strictly statutory.
The parties cannot expand or reduce those rights by contract, although in some situations they could waive their right to appeal.
Consent judgments cannot be appealed as of right, but they can be appealed if permission is obtained under R.
As in this appeal, binding JDR agreements often confirm a limitation on appeal rights, which may in some cases amount to a full waiver of those appeal rights.
[19] Permission will not easily be obtained to appeal a consent judgment arising from a JDR session.

The premise of the JDR process is that the parties have agreed to resolving their dispute outside the normal adversarial process, and the party seeking permission will have to explain why he or she should be entitled to step around that agreement: Steenberg v Steenberg, 2023 ABCA 132 at para.
13; Laanep v Lawson, 2021 ABCA 214 at para.
Mere dissatisfaction with the outcome, or that a different result may have emerged following a full trial, are insufficient reasons for an appeal.

The applicant will have to show some important question of law or precedent, a reasonable prospect of success, and that an appeal would not prejudice the other party: Basaraba v Tibbetts, 2021 ABCA 369 at para.
[20] In this appeal the requirement for permission was raised.

By the time the application to strike and the cross-application for permission were brought, oral argument of the appeal was ready to be scheduled.
As a result, a single duty judge directed that the cross-applications and the appeal itself be argued concurrently.
The application to strike and the cross application for permission to appeal are, however, essentially moot and no formal adjudication of them is required.

By using terms such as “jurisdiction”, “absence of notice”, and “absence of an application” the appellant analogizes the JDR process to the ordinary court adjudicative process.
However, while the JDR process may be annexed to the ordinary processes of the court, it is distinct.
[22] A JDR judge has a wide discretion as to how to conduct the session.
Subject to any agreement or understanding of the parties and the Rules on JDRs, the judge is not bound by the rules of evidence, nor is he or she obliged to follow any particular procedure.
While it is expected that a certain level of procedural fairness will be observed at the JDR, the process does not assume any requirement of formal notice, nor does it require formal “applications”.
[23] In this case it became apparent that the letter written by the JDR judge on November 9, 2022 was unclear.
The parties appeared in docket court to outline the problem and were referred back to the JDR judge.
The appearance before the JDR judge on July 12, 2023 was to resolve that ambiguity.
No further notice was required, nor was there a need for a formal application.
On the facts shown by this record, there was no inherent procedural unfairness involved.

Part of the allegation that the JDR judge “exceeded his jurisdiction” also relates to his clarification of the ambiguity in the November 9, 2022 letter.
[25] There will undoubtedly come a point where a binding JDR judge should be regarded as having spent his or her mandate, or what would be described in a more formal context as becoming “functus”.
The stage at which that occurs would depend on the circumstances, but thereafter no further variations to the binding JDR opinion are appropriate.
That point was not, however, reached in this case.
[26] First of all, the order of March 25, 2022 could not exhaust the JDR process, because it expressly provided in clause 16 that the parties had consented to the continuation of the process.
Further information was to be provided to the JDR judge, following which he would render an opinion on the outstanding issues, including retroactive support and arrears.
[27] The letter of November 9, 2022 was intended to resolve the outstanding issues, but the JDR judge agreed it contained ambiguities.
In such a circumstance, it is not objectionable for the JDR judge to clarify his original intention.
Even though the processes are different, it is noteworthy that until a judgment or order is actually entered, a trial judge has the ability to vary or modify it: R.
A judge presiding at a binding JDR cannot have any less flexibility than that.
[28] The appellant argues that two weeks after the letter of November 9, 2022 the mandate of the binding JDR judge ended.
After that point, R.
4.21 prevented him having any further involvement in the process, at least without consent.
This argument is based on clause 12 of the Agreement: 12.

(judgement) is not issued at the conclusion of the JDR, both parties agree that if they are unable to come to agreement on settling the minutes of the Judgment arising from the decision made by the Justice within two weeks of the conclusion of the JDR either party may apply to the Justice to finalize such terms and the Justice shall grant a Judgment containing the terms the Justice determines are consistent with the decision made irrespective of whether or not a party agrees with those terms.
This clause, however, does not limit the mandate of the binding JDR judge.

It should be interpreted against the background that access to judges is limited, and it often would be difficult to schedule within two weeks.
On a proper interpretation, the phrase “within two weeks of the conclusion”, relates back to the phrase “unable to come to agreement on settling the minutes”.

Clause 12 means if the “parties … are unable to come to agreement within two weeks of the conclusion of the JDR on settling the minutes of the Judgment” they may apply for directions.
This interpretation gives the binding JDR judge the same flexibility as would be provided to a trial judge under R.

paragraphs.text: (1) An arrangement for a judicial dispute resolution process may be made only with the agreement of the participating parties and, before engaging in a judicial dispute resolution process, and subject to the directions of the presiding judge, the participating parties must agree to the extent possible on at least the following: (a) that every party necessary to participate in the process has agreed to do so, unless there is sufficient reason not to have complete agreement; (b) rules to be followed in the process, including rules respecting (i) the nature of the process, (ii) the matters to be the subject of the process, (iii) the manner in which the process will be conducted, (iv) the date on which and the location and time at which the process will occur, (v) the role of the judge and any outcome expected of that role, (vi) any practice or procedure related to the process, including exchange of materials, before, at or after the process, (vii) who will participate in the process, which must include persons who have authority to agree on a resolution of the dispute, unless otherwise agreed, and (viii) any other matter appropriate to the process, the parties or the dispute. (2) The parties who agree on the proposed judicial dispute resolution process are entitled to participate in the process. (3) The parties to a proposed judicial dispute resolution process may request that a judge named by the parties participate in the process.

sentences.text: Confidentiality and use of information

paragraphs.text: (1) A judicial dispute resolution process is a confidential process intended to facilitate the resolution of a dispute. (2) Unless the parties otherwise agree in writing, statements made or documents generated for or in the judicial dispute resolution process with a view to resolving the dispute (a) are privileged and are made or generated without prejudice, (b) must be treated by the parties and participants in the process as confidential and may only be used for the purpose of that dispute resolution process, and (c) may not be referred to, presented as evidence or relied on, and are not admissible in a subsequent application or proceeding in the same action or in any other action, or in proceedings of a judicial or quasi-judicial nature. (3) Subrule (2) does not apply to the documents referred to in rule 4.19. (4) Subrule (2) does not prevent the use of statements made or documents generated for or in the judicial dispute resolution process to prove the fact that a settlement was reached or the terms of a settlement. paragraphs.text: (1) The judge facilitating a judicial dispute resolution process in an action must not hear or decide any subsequent application, proceeding or trial in the action without the written agreement of every party and the agreement of the judge. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 4.22:1 Rule 4.22 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 4.22. 1. Overview In Aski Construction Ltd. v. Markos, 2017 ABCA 341, 2017 CarswellAlta 1845 Madam Justice Schutz gave this overview of the law relating to security for costs: 7 Security for costs is a discretionary order that balances the reasonable expectations and rights of the parties to come to a just and reasonable conclusion: Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367 at para 8. A single appeal judge may award security for costs in accordance with Rules 14.67(1) and 4.22 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010. Rule 4.22 states that the court may order a party to provide security for cost if the court considers it just and reasonable to do so, taking into account all of the following: a) whether it is likely the applicant for the order will be able to enforce an order or judgment against assets in Alberta; b) the ability of the respondent to the application to pay the costs award; c) the merits of the action in which the application is filed; d) whether an order to give security for payment of a costs award would unduly prejudice the respondent's ability to continue the action; e) any other matter the Court considers appropriate. 8 The onus is on the applicant to prove these factors weigh in their favour. In previous decisions from this Court, concerns regarding a party's ability to pay costs coupled with modest prospects of an appeal's success have been sufficient to justify granting an application for security for costs: see for example Matty v Rammasoot, 2013 ABCA 170. 9 However, the analysis does not end there. The Court has the discretion to refuse to order security for costs where the application has not been made promptly and there is a risk of resultant prejudice: Castillo v Go, 2002 ABCA 271 at paras 14, 18, 317 AR 195; Collins v Collins (Estate of), 2005 ABCA 41 at para 20. This is particularly the case when delay in bringing the application for security for costs is unexplained: Marathon Canada Ltd v Enron Canada Corp, 2008 ABCA 424 at para 10, 446 AR 88. In Parker v. Parker, 2019 ABCA 114, 2019 CarswellAlta 574, 89 Alta. L.R. (6th) 104, Justice Greckol said: [4] A security for costs order is discretionary and balances the reasonable expectations of the parties with their rights in order to arrive at a just and reasonable outcome: Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367 (CanLII) at para 8. The onus rests with the applicant to establish that the factors in r 4.22 are met: Aski Construction Ltd v Markos, 2017 ABCA 341 (CanLII) at para 8. A failure to pay costs awarded in previous trial court processes, along with a demonstrated inability to pay costs if an appeal is unsuccessful, will be sufficient to grant a security for costs order in most cases: DataNet Information Systems, Inc v Belzil, 2011 ABCA 40 (CanLII) (chambers) at para 4. “Access to justice does not equate to access to civil processes without fear of costs consequences”: ibid. This statement was referred to with approval in Patton v. Horse Racing Alberta, 2019 ABCA 182, 2019 CarswellAlta 928 at paragraph 11. In Skolney v. Nisha, 2018 ABCA 78, 2018 CarswellAlta 342, 10 R.F.L. (8th) 34, Justice Greckol said: [21] Granting security for costs is a discretionary decision, which requires a judge to look to the equities of the case at bar before making an order. Rule 4.22 states the Court “may” order security for costs if it “considers it just and reasonable to do so”. … That comment was also referred to with approval in Patton v. Horse Racing Alberta, 2019 ABCA 182, 2019 CarswellAlta 928, at paragraph 13. Also see the annotations under Rule 14.67. 2. Merits of the Action In Bechir v. Gowling Lafleur Henderson LLP, 2017 ABQB 214, 2017 CarswellAlta 566, Justice Jeffrey discussed “merits of the action” as that term is used in R. 4.22(c): 12 As a general rule, the principles governing the consideration of Rule 4.22(c) are: … 2. The court must attempt to look at the merits of the action, as difficult as that may be on an interlocutory application; 3. The greater the likelihood of success for the plaintiff (if that can be reasonably assessed) the more the court should consider the potential unjustness of preventing a meritorious claim from proceeding; 4. The converse is true: the smaller the likelihood of success for the plaintiff (if that can be reasonably assessed) the slower the court should be in denying security when security would otherwise be appropriate (1251165 Alberta Ltd v Wells Fargo Equipment Co, 2013 ABQB 533 at para 44) 13 For a security for cost application, the degree of rigour to the court's assessment of the merits under Rule 4.22(c) varies depending on how far into the litigation that the application for security for costs is brought: see PM&C Specialist Contractors Inc v Horton CBI Limited, 2015 ABQB 248 at para 15. The later in the proceedings the application for security for costs is brought, the more in-depth the merits of the case will be examined. Early in the proceedings, “it is difficult for any court … to weigh the merits. It has heard no evidence and must attempt to rely on the submissions of counsel that arise from their pleadings and the questioning that has taken place to this point”: Provalcid Inc v Graff, 2014 ABQB 453 at para 97. Therefore, if an application for security for costs is brought early in the proceedings, “it is neither possible, nor desirable, for the Court at this stage to determine which party's case is stronger”: Attila Dogan Construction v AMEC Americas Limited, 2011 ABQB 175 at para 17. 14 The consensus in the Alberta case law is that the merits of the case are relatively unimportant for applications brought early in the proceedings. In Provalcid Inc, at para 97, Justice Yamauchi quoted with approval the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal decision in Wall v Horn Abbot Ltd (1999), 176 NSR (2d) 96 at para 59: Second, while the merits of the plaintiff's case are relevant and may be considered, they should only be considered on the basis of undisputed facts, the pleadings, etc. and not on the basis of seriously disputed facts or assessments of credibility. Third, consideration of the merits should only be decisive where they are clear and obvious. In short, the law relating to consideration of the merits on interlocutory applications for security for costs is in harmony with the general reluctance to assess the merits of a claim or defence, other than in obvious cases, before trial. [emphasis added] 15 Further, in Xpress Lube & Car Wash Ltd v Gill, 2011 ABQB 457 at para 11, Justice Hall stated that: In regard to Rule 4.22(c), the Court notes that neither action has proceeded through questioning. Each action makes allegations which, if proven, could ground a judgment; that is to say, valid causes of action are alleged. In these two cases it is simply too early for the Court to be persuaded that the actions do or do not have merit. Therefore, nothing turns on this subrule at present. Following the completion of questioning, this consideration may have greater weight. [emphasis added] 16 In a recent decision, Alberta (Attorney General) v Alberta Power, 2017 ABQB 195 at para 26, Chief Justice Wittmann summarized the general principles applicable to the scope of a cross-examination on affidavit in Alberta. The last of those is: 6. The principle of proportionality is a consideration and undertakings otherwise answerable had the deponent had the information available at oral questioning ought to be answered provided the provision of the information would not be “overly onerous” and would likely significantly help the Court in the determination of the application: Dow Chemical Canada Inc[2008] A.J. No. 1195 at para 5; Rozak Estate at para 41; PM&C Specialists Contractors at paras 9, 21. 17 While the merits of the case must be considered by the Court in a security for costs application under Rule 4.22(c), the Court does not attempt to determine which case is stronger. Rather, if both parties establish a reasonably meritorious case on the pleadings and available evidence, Rule 4.22(c) should be a neutral consideration in the application. 3. The Rule Can Apply To A Defendant In Toronto Dominion Bank v. Suitel Canada Executive Suites Corp., 2011 ABQB 519, 2011 CarswellAlta 2250, 527 A.R. 97, Justice Yamauchi said, at paragraphs 25-26: 25 At the outset, it should be noted that there is nothing preventing this Court from requiring Valerio, a defendant in this action, to post security for costs. The opening words of Alberta Rules of Court r. 4.22, speak of “a party.” It is not limited to plaintiffs. The wording in the Alberta Rules of Court that preceded the current rules, used the word “plaintiff” when it referred to a person against whom an order for security for costs could be sought. The Alberta Legislature made an amendment to that rule to allow security for costs against “any party” where the court finds it just and reasonable to do so in the circumstances. The Alberta Court of Appeal in Rushton v. Condominium Plan No. 8820668, 1998 ABCA 217, 219 A.R. 51 at 58, said that this amendment was enacted with the specific intent to make some defendants give security. 26 This Court must, however, exercise caution when it considers whether it should make such an award, as “no party should have to give security for costs as a condition of simply defending itself”: Toronto Dominion Bank v. Szilagyi Farms Ltd. (1998), 65 O.R. (2d) 433, [1988] O.J. No. 1223 at para. 21 (C.A.), citing Re Percy & Kelly Nickel, Cobalt, and Chrome Iron Mining Co. (1876), 2 Ch. D. 531. In 1400467 Alberta Ltd. v. Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439, 2014 CarswellAlta 1208, 55 C.P.C. (7th) 303, Madam Justice Veit said, at paragraphs 11–13: 11 Although Rule 4.22 clearly allows a court to order security for costs against a defendant, case law makes it clear that, even where a defendant fails to satisfy any of the specific factors mentioned in the rule, the issuance of such an order is far from automatic. On the contrary, the general rule concerning the posting of security for costs by defendants is this: a plaintiff cannot call upon the defendant, even one resident out of the jurisdiction, to provide security for the plaintiff's costs. 12 The earliest explanation that I have been able to find of the policy underpinning this general rule in Canadian law was articulated in Lever: 8 The question is: Are there cases where the plaintiff “by law or practice” is entitled to obtain an order for security for costs? The particular provisions of rule 5(1) deal with applications by defendants. … 12 Reference having been made to England and Ontario I have looked into the practice in those jurisdictions. In England the general rule is stated by Jessel, M.R., in In re Percy and Kelly Nickel, Cobalt and Chrome Iron Mining Company, [1875-76] 2 Ch.D. 53]: The principle is well established that a person instituting legal proceedings in this country, and being abroad, so that no adverse order could be effectually made against him if unsuccessful, is by the rules of the court compelled to give security for costs. That is perfectly well established and a perfectly reasonable principle; but it does not apply to a defendant or respondent who is brought here to defend himself. If the person who institutes proceedings chooses to bring here people out of the jurisdiction, he must, in the first instance, consider whether or not it is worth his while to do so, even if he does not get costs. He must take upon himself the risk of being unable to recover his costs, and cannot be allowed to say that the defendant whom he has chosen to bring here is not to defend himself. 13 In more recent days in England the principle remains the same. It is said by Lord Greene, M.R., in Naamalooze v. Bank of England, [1948] 1 All E.R. 465, at p. 468: That seems to me to be the right principle, that a defendant who is exercising the right of any defendant to defend himself against attack ought to be allowed to do so and not prevented or hampered by being ordered to give security. 14 In Ontario the same principle is adopted in Knickerbocker Trust Company of New York et al v. Webster (1896), 17 P.R. 189, and Sample et al v. McLaughlin et al (1897), 17 P.R. 490. Many more recent cases accept Knickerbocker as the authority for the general principle hereinbefore stated. 15 In my opinion, the practice, as in England, is and ought to be the practice and law in Nova Scotia. 16 It becomes clear that this is a case for application of the general principle that a plaintiff who is the real actor and initiator of the litigation cannot call upon the defendant, resident out of the jurisdiction, to provide security for the plaintiff's costs. (Emphasis added) 13 So far as I am aware, the analysis set out in Lever has never been criticized or over-ridden in Canadian law. Nor does the very general language of Rule 4.22, and of its immediate predecessor, create a dramatic departure from what has always been the approach of Canadian courts to security for costs; a revision to the Rules was necessary only in order to explicitly accommodate the relatively rare situations in which a plaintiff, or a defendant within the province, could properly be ordered to post security for costs. Casual references to the general principle as set out in Lever are often made in contemporary decisions in Alberta and elsewhere: see, for example, by the Ontario Court of Appeal in Szylagyi Farms at para. 21, and by my colleague Yamauchi J. in Suitel Canada at para. 26. Indeed, the general rule is merely an application of common sense: a defendant has no choice about being a party to the litigation whereas a plaintiff typically has the choice, not only to commence litigation, but also, where to commence litigation. In this case, the plaintiffs could have sued the defendants in Saskatchewan: the choice of law, and especially the choice of forum, contracts which the principal defendants executed and which made it obvious that Alberta was the forum conveniens were contracts that benefitted the plaintiffs and were therefore contracts the benefit of which the plaintiffs could have chosen to forego. In every case, a prospective plaintiff who has a viable cause of action must make a decision about whether suing will throw good money after bad. In some cases, a defendant must make an analogous choice: sometimes judgment will be conceded at an early stage merely so as not to incur further, larger, legal expenses which can never be recovered. In other situations, a defendant allows judgment to go against it not because it does not have a defence, but because it doesn't have the finances to allow it to defend. If a plaintiff doesn't think a defendant has exigible assets, its most obvious relief is not to sue that defendant. It would clearly be unfair to grant a plaintiff security for costs when doing so will effectively give the plaintiff judgment but where the only negative thing against the defendant is that it is impecunious. In HLFN Industry Relations Corporation v. Horseman, 2019 ABQB 564, 2019 CarswellAlta 1533, Justice Ross said: [15] Generally, a plaintiff cannot call on defendants to post security for costs: 1400467 Alberta Ltd v Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439 (CanLII), at paras 11-12. However, there is no bar for a plaintiff/defendant by counterclaim obtaining security for costs against defendants/plaintiffs by counterclaim on their counterclaim. “Defendants do not have to put up security to defend, but they may if they are advancing a counterclaim”: 1251165 Alberta Ltd v Wells Fargo Equipment Company Ltd, 2013 ABQB 533 (CanLII), at para 35 (“Wells Fargo”). [16] The Court should follow a two-step process: first, considering the factors in Rule 4.22; and second, considering whether it is just and reasonable to grant security for costs: WestJet v ELS Marketing Inc, 2016 ABQB 172 (CanLII), paras 25-26. In RDX Technologies Corporation v. Appel, 2019 ABCA 338, 2019 CarswellAlta 1923, Justice Feehan said: [32] Orders for security for costs to be paid by defendants are unusual, particularly where the plaintiff has chosen to litigate in a jurisdiction where the defendants have no presence and have no choice in being parties to the action (see Jager Estate v Deadman, 2019 ABCA 99, paras 31-32; 1400467 Alberta Ltd v Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439, paras 11–13, 591 AR 40; Donaldson International Livestock Ltd v Znamensky Selekcionno-Gibridny Center LLC, 2010 ONCA 137, paras 13-14, 101 OR (3d) 314, and Bouzari v Bahremani, 2014 ONCA 476, paras 7 and 15, 406 DLR (4th) 392). [33] On an application by a plaintiff, “even where a defendant fails to satisfy any of the specific factors mentioned in the rule, the issuance of … an order [for security for costs] is far from automatic.” On the contrary, the general rule is that a plaintiff cannot call upon a defendant, “even one resident out of the jurisdiction, to provide security for the plaintiff's costs” (Adderley, para 11) (see historically: In Re Percy and Kelly Nickel, Cobalt and Chrome Iron Mining Co, [1875-76] 2 Ch D 531; Naamalooze v Bank of England, [1948] 1 All ER 465 at p 468, Knickerbocker Trust Co of New York v Webster (1896), 17 Ont PR 189 (CA); Sample v McLachlan (1897), 17 Ont PR 490 (Div Ct); Lever v Harrietha (1971), 4 NSR (2d) 306, paras 8, 12–16). [34] A defendant “has no choice about being a party to the litigation whereas a plaintiff typically has the choice, not only to commence litigation, but also, where to commence litigation” (Adderley, para 13). [35] These observations are particularly critical where there is a serious contest between the parties as to the appropriate forum for the litigation between them. 4. Onus Is First On Applicant; It Can Shift To Respondent In Toronto Dominion Bank v. Suitel Canada Executive Suites Corp., 2011 ABQB 519, 2011 CarswellAlta 2250, 527 A.R. 97, the Plaintiff sought a security for costs order against a Defendant (Valerio). A dispute arose as to the residence of Valerio. Justice Yamauchi said, at paragraph 28: 28 There is contradictory evidence as to where Valerio resides. The fact that he has a joint interest in the Condo belies an allegation that he is ordinarily resident in the Dominican Republic. On the other hand, Valerio deposes that he and his spouse own a house in the Dominican Republic, which points to their residing in that country. We must remember that TD Bank has the onus to make out its case under Alberta Rules of Court r. 4.22, before the burden shifts to Valerio: Hildebrandt v. Fire on the Mountain Productions Inc., 2001 ABQB 301, 287 A.R. 363 at paras. 11 - 12 (Master). Without more evidence, this Court cannot find that Valerio is a non-resident. His Lordship then explained that once an applicant has satisfied its onus to bring itself within the Rule, the onus shifts to the respondent to show why an order ought not to be made. At paragraph 31, Yamauchi, J. said: 31 TD Bank has satisfied the onus on it to bring itself within Alberta Rules of Court r. 4.22. Thus, the evidentiary burden shifts to Valerio to show that this Court should not post security for costs. Why this shift? Valerio is the only person who knows whether there is any reason why this Court should not order him to post security for costs: Besler at para. 15; Steffanson v. Richardson Greenshields of Canada Ltd., [1992] A.J. No. 929, 135 A.R. 55 at 56 (C.A.). In Mudrick Capital Management v. Wright, 2018 ABQB 648, 2018 CarswellAlta 1855, 77 Alta. L.R. (6th) 421, Justice Yamauchi again discussed the onus of proof under both R. 4.22 and section 254 of the Business Corporations Act: [8] In Trimove Inc v Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50 (CanLII) at para 108, 44 CBR (6th) 5, Nielsen J said the following: … Whether an application for security for costs is brought pursuant to s. 254 of the BCA or pursuant to Rule 4.22, the onus of proof does not change. The applicant seeking security for costs bears the initial onus to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the respondent will be unable to pay its costs if the defence is successful. If the applicant satisfies this onus, the evidentiary burden shifts to the respondent to show why the Court should not exercise its discretion to make such an Order against it. [9] In the case at bar, the applicant Defendants bear the initial onus. If the evidentiary burden shifts, the respondent Plaintiffs must establish why this Court should not exercise its discretion to make an order for security for costs, in the case of ABCA s 254 or whether it would be just and reasonable for this Court to grant an order for security for costs, in the case of Rules r 4.22. In either case, the decision of whether to require the respondent to pay security for costs is discretionary: Amex Electrical Ltd v 726934 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 66 (CanLII) at paras 71-72, 582 AR 304, 99 Alta LR (5th) 1. In Commercial Construction Supply Ltd. v. Ghost Riders Farm Inc., 2016 ABQB 166, 2016 CarswellAlta 495, the defendants applied for an order requiring the plaintiff (CCS) to post security for costs. Justice Nielsen said at paragraphs 22–25: 22 CCS is a body corporate and, as such, s. 254 of the BCA applies. In all other cases not subject to other statutory enactments, Rule 4.22 applies. Whether an application is brought pursuant to s. 254 of the BCA or pursuant to Rule 4.22, the onus of proof does not change. The applicant seeking security for costs bears the initial onus to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the respondent will be unable to pay its costs if the defence is successful. If the applicant satisfies this onus, the evidentiary burden shifts to the respondent to show why the Court should not exercise its discretion to make such an Order against it: Amex Electrical Ltd v 726934 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 66, 582 AR 304; Provalcid Inc v Graff, 2014 ABQB 453, 591 AR 117. 23 In Amex, Wakeling J. (as he then was) set out two non-exhaustive lists of factors that might increase or decrease the likelihood that a court will award security for costs. Factors favouring the granting of an Order for security for costs include (para 74): a) the respondent is a corporation and has no assets in Alberta; b) the respondent is a corporation and the assets it has in Alberta are of a nature or value that there is a substantial risk that the applicant may not be able to recover any costs award likely to be granted to it; c) the likelihood the respondent will receive judgment against the applicant is low; d) a security for costs Order will not prevent the respondent from prosecuting its action; e) the applicant is not seeking security for steps already taken; f) if the applicant has counterclaimed, and the issues raised by the counterclaim and the claim are different, this will not deter a court from granting security for costs; g) the applicant has applied for a security for costs Order at the earliest opportunity; and h) the resolution of the issues presented by the respondent's action is not important to the greater community. 24 Factors weighing against the granting of an Order for security for costs include (para 75): (a) the applicant failed to apply for security for costs at the earliest opportunity; (b) the applicant seeks security for costs of steps already taken; (c) the respondent has assets in Alberta of a nature and value that there is little risk the applicant will be unable to recover any cost award likely to be granted to the applicant; (d) the likelihood the respondent will receive judgment against the applicant is high; (e) the shareholders of a corporation, which has no assets in Alberta or the assets it has in Alberta are of a nature and value that there is a substantial risk the applicant may not be able to recover any costs award likely to be granted to it, have assets in Alberta that would be sufficient to meet any costs award likely to be granted and have offered to provide personal guarantees; (f) a security for costs Order will prevent the respondent from prosecuting its action; (g) the applicant has counterclaimed and the issues raised by the counterclaim and the claim are the same or the counterclaim adds significantly to the action, with the potential to prolong discoveries and trial; and (h) the resolution of the issue presented by the respondent's action is important to the community. 25 Yamauchi, J. in Provalcid commented on the foregoing factors and explained the interplay of s. 254 of the BCA and Rule 4.22: 92 It is worthwhile to note that many of the cases that Wakeling J cited for the propositions he put forth involve an interpretation of Rules r 4.22, or its predecessor. There is logic to this approach inasmuch as the court, when considering whether the applicant has met the standard of proof required in BCA s 254, must consider the same factors when it is considering whether the applicant has met the standard of proof under Rules r 4.22, viz, those contained in Rules rr 4.22(a) through (e). The difference, however, is the ultimate determination the court must make when weighing those factors. Under BCA s 254, the court must determine whether the body corporate is “unable to pay the costs of a successful defendant.” Under Rules r 4.22, the court must determine whether it is “just and reasonable” to require the respondent to provide security for costs. 93 Accordingly, it is appropriate for this Court to consider cases that were decided under Rules r 4.22, but only to determine whether [the applicant] has met his onus under BCA s 254.
