As Mr Justice Hall pointed out in Xpress Lube, the test under s 254 is more stringent. The test is whether the applicant has established on the balance of probabilities that the corporate plaintiff will be unable to pay (Amex Electrical Ltd v 726934 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 66 at para 55 and authorities cited therein). 40 I agree this is a more stringent standard than R 4.22. Section 254 does not mean the defendant “will be unable to collect in Alberta” or the plaintiff will be unwilling to pay. There is no evidence that Autoweld does not have a viable ongoing business capable of generating revenue. It is not possible to conclude on these facts that Autoweld “will be unable to pay”. 41 The purpose of the corporate specific sections was to change, in the case of corporations, the long-standing rule that impecunious plaintiffs could not be forced to post security for costs (see para 20-21 above). It follows that an applicant has to demonstrate some evidence of inability to pay before an onus arises on the respondent to show some reason that the Court should decline to make an order. His Lordship specifically disagreed with the proposition that section 254 of the Business Corporations Act displaces Rule 4.22 (though he applied section 254 of the Act because that was the foundation of the Defendant's application). Justice Eamon said: 49 I have decided this case on s 254 only for the procedural reasons described in para 46 above. Nothing in my reasons should be taken as agreement with the line of cases that says s 254 is the exclusive provision for security for costs where a corporation is a plaintiff (or perhaps a defendant), and R 4.22 does not apply (Amex at paras 6, 58 and 69; see also Provalcid Inc v Graff, 2014 ABQB 453 at para 87; Pinto Ventures Ltd v Soost, 2016 ABQB 454 at para 160, aff'd on other gnds, 2017 ABCA 25; Geophysical Service Incorporated v Encana Corporation, 2016 ABQB 49 at para 20 (where the parties agreed that s 254 applied); Commercial Construction Supply Ltd v Ghost Riders Farm Inc, 2016 ABQB 166 at para 22; John Barlot Architect Ltd v Atrium Square Investments Ltd, 2017 ABQB 749 at para 47.) 50 Similarly, the Plaintiff says the only test for security for costs is s 254 of the BCA, citing Amex and cases which have followed it including Pinto Ventures, which it notes was a decision upheld on appeal. I note that the security for costs award was not in issue on appeal, and the appellate decision does not affirm the Amex line of cases. 51 I note the authority to the contrary is Xpress Lube at para 16, holding that s 254 and R 4.22 are alternative grounds for awarding security for costs against a corporate litigant. There were cases decided before Amex which applied s 254 and R 4.22 (or its predecessors) as alternative grounds for awarding security. An example is Autoweld, where Mr Justice McMahon found that s 254 was not met but security was nevertheless just and reasonable under R 4.22. 52 The Amex line of cases is contrary to my own views on the matter. The company specific provisions acted as a back stop, reflecting a policy determination that impecunious companies should not receive the same generous treatment as impecunious individuals. I would not construe a price of incorporation as a bonus of immunity from R 4.22. It seems doubtful to me that in 1901, when the provision was added to corporate law in the territories, or by 1981 when the provision was reworded, the Legislature intended to displace the Court's broad power to deal with the highly variable fact patterns where security might be required (for example, where a litigant brings the same claim in multiple jurisdictions or acts vexatiously), or displace the Court's long standing power to require security where a non-resident brought proceedings. 53 It may be worthwhile for that point to be authoritatively clarified. If corporations can only be compelled to provide security where an applicant can prove inability to pay, the values underlying the Rules and the Court's litigation management tools will be substantially damaged. But, in this case, the parties agreed to apply s 254 and the question was not argued. The Merits of the Action Rule 4.22(c) provides that one of the factors the Court must consider in a security for costs application is “the merits of the action in which the application is filed”. The previous rule (594) required that the application “be supported by an affidavit of the defendant or his agent, who can speak positively as to the facts, alleging that there is a good defence to the action on the merits and specifying the nature thereof.” In Attila Dogan Construction v. AMEC Americas Ltd., 2011 ABQB 175, 2011 CarswellAlta 407, 504 A.R. 295, 49 Alta. L.R. (5th) 212, Chief Justice Wittmann concluded that the new Rule requires “an inquiry into the merits”. At paragraphs 17 and 18, his Lordship said: 17 Both parties have cited authorities under old Rules 593 and 594. Those Rules did not, in the manner of Rule 4.22, set out a list of factors to be considered in determining whether security should be granted. Rule 594 provided that an application for security for costs should be supported by an affidavit of the defendant or his agent, who can speak positively as to the facts, alleging that there is a good defence to the action on the merits and specifying the nature thereof. It is AD's [AD is the Plaintiff] contention that Rule 4.22 mandates a more detailed inquiry into the relative strengths of each party's position and a higher standard than a reasonably arguable defence. Even if this is so, it does not follow that, as AD suggests, the appropriate and determinative question is which party has a stronger case. This is a highly complex claim What Rule 4.22 requires is an inquiry into the merits. In my view, this suggests that a reasonably meritorious defence, when considered together with the other factors set out in Rule 4.22, is sufficient to weigh in favour of granting security for costs. It is neither possible, nor desirable, for the Court at this stage to determine which party's case is stronger. 18 AMEC has raised a reasonably meritorious defence, grounded in evidence relating to the ability of AD to fulfil its obligations to JorMag independent of the alleged gross negligence of AMEC, and grounded in several contractual provisions that appear to be pertinent to the claims made by AD. This is sufficient for the purposes of Rule 4.22(c), especially where, as here, AD has elected not to put forward any evidence on this application. In relation to the factor “the merits of the action in which the application is filed”, Justice McMahon, in Autoweld Systems Ltd. v. CRC-Evans Pipeline International, Inc., 2011 ABQB 265, 2011 CarswellAlta 679, 504 A.R. 288, [2011] A.J. No. 460; leave to appeal refused 2011 CarswellAlta 1355, 2011 ABCA 243, 515 A.R. 6, 57 Alta. L.R. (5th) 429, 532 W.A.C. 6, said, at paragraph 22: 22 … There is insufficient basis at this early stage to determine which party has the better prospect of success in this commercial dispute Autoweld has filed no affidavit evidence. CRC-Evans has filed an affidavit sworn by one of its officers and a named defendant in which he deposes to a good defence on the merits. Significant detail is provided. Autoweld relies upon its cross-examination on this and other affidavits to establish the merits of its claim. The parties have litigated related issues since 1996. It is a reasonable inference that commercial bodies, well advised, will not litigate hopeless causes for fifteen years. The former Rule 594 required an affidavit from the applicant alleging a good defence on the merits and specifying its nature. I do not see that Rule 4.22(c) raises the bar or demands a higher standard or a more detailed inquiry into the merits. When the motion is brought before document production and before oral questioning, none of that is realistic. What the new factor does do is broaden the consideration from only the merits of the defence to the merits of the action. It therefore requires a balanced view of the entire action as it then appears. On the material before me I am satisfied that there is merit, i.e., that both the claimant and the defence raise serious and arguable issues. 9. Purpose of Rule The general purpose of the rule was stated by Andrekson J. as follows: In reviewing R. 593(1), it is clear that the rule was designed to protect the Defendant and to ensure that the Plaintiffs are able to answer the costs at the end of the proceedings. Tkaczuk v. Frocan (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 4 at 7 (Q.B.). The security for costs rules are not designed to fund a lawsuit. Nor can the Rules of Court relating to security for costs be combined with the prospective right to indemnity to obtain immediate funding. Security for costs rules provide for security; they do not envisage funding in advance before the cause of action is decided. Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1989), 68 Alta. L.R. (2d) 194 at 202 (C.A.). 15. Do Not Factor In Rules Regarding Double Costs In Home Exchange (Alberta) Ltd. v. Goodyear Canada Inc., 2001 ABQB 673, 2001 CarswellAlta 1011, 291 A.R. 295, a defendant applied for security for costs in an amount that assumed that “Goodyear will beat a formal Offer of Judgment and thereby earn an entitlement to double costs.” In rejecting that approach, Lee J. said, at p. 300: … Taking Offers of Settlement into consideration would merely promote self-serving offers, thereby discouraging true settlement efforts. For example, any Defendant could seek “double security” for costs on the basis that, if it is completely successful at trial, it will beat a nuisance value offer, and offers might be made for no other purpose than to escalate and double the claim for security for costs. Further, the purpose of security for costs is financial in nature, that is, to protect a litigant's position with respect to costs. The purpose of the double costs provisions in the Rules of Court is punitive in nature, that is, to promote settlement by imposing consequences for failing to settle. It is not proper to import a punitive purpose into the security for costs provisions. I further conclude that it is speculative to suggest at this stage that the Plaintiff will be punished by an award of costs, before the matter is even ready for trial. 16. When Security for Costs is Returnable in the Face of an Appeal In Polansky Electronics Ltd. v. AGT Ltd., 2000 ABCA 46, 2000 CarswellAlta 109, 277 A.R. 55, 80 Alta. L.R. (3d) 57, the plaintiff Polansky sued the defendant AGT for patent infringement. The plaintiff was ordered to post, and did post, $75,000 as security for costs for the trial. At trial the plaintiff was successful, and the defendant appealed. The plaintiff sought the return of the $75,000 pending the appeal. The Court of Appeal refused to order the return of the security for costs in the absence of evidence showing that the circumstances of the plaintiff had changed since the granting of the original order. At p. 58, Russell J.A. said: The appeal is simply another step in the litigation process and it is possible that the Appellate court may making (sic) a ruling opposite to that of the trial judge with respect to the matter of costs. The order for security of costs is prima facie evidence that when it was granted Polansky was in some respect financially insecure. Thus, in the absence of evidence from Polansky showing a change in those circumstances, if money deposited for security for costs is returned, it can be inferred that there is still some risk that if the appeal is allowed the money will not be there to answer the purpose for which its payment was ordered. Therefore, Polansky is not entitled to the return of the $75,000 at this time. 17. Delay in Bringing Application An application for security for costs must be made reasonably promptly: Wall v. Wells, [1926] 37 B.C.R. 445 (C.A.); Shea's Hotel Sales Ltd. v. Dell Hotel Ltd., supra; Whitfield v. Thompson (1977), 3 B.C.L.R. 63 (S.C.); Allwise Const. Ltd. v. Tynan (1977), 5 B.C.L.R. 20 (Co. Ct.); Frank Hillis Logging Co. v. Hoeya Sound Logging Ltd., [1971] 2 W.W.R. 471 (B.C. C.A.). Failure to do so is not necessarily fatal to the application. If a plaintiff is lulled into the false belief that he may proceed with the action without being called upon to advance security and does act upon that belief, a subsequent application for security will not be allowed, at least as to past costs. Before such delay doctrine can be applied, there must be some indication that the delay has had the effect of leading the plaintiff into a false sense of security or has worked to his prejudice. United Paint & Coating Canada Ltd. v. St. Laurent (1980), 13 Alta. L.R. (2d) 134 (Master), at 140, per Master Funduk. And McDonald J. has said: Even if there has been some delay on the part of the defendant in the present case, the order should be granted unless the plaintiff shows that it suffered some prejudice from the delay or was induced into believing that it was safe in incurring costs without risking facing an order for security for costs. In Officine Vittorio Ceccoli, S.P.A. v. British Columbia Hydro & Power Authority, [1971] 3 W.W.R. 81 (B.C. C.A.), Bull, J.A., said at p. 83: In the absence of any time limitation imposed by rule, delay of itself is not in my opinion a valid answer to the motion. It has been held many times that applications for security for costs must be brought promptly but the reason for this is, I think, that delay may induce the belief in a plaintiff that he may be reasonably safe incurring costs on his own behalf without the risk of being confronted with an order for security with which he may be unable to comply and thus be compelled to throw away the expense theretofore incurred in the prosecution of his case. Determining the amount is highly discretionary, and must be done on a case by case basis: Beacon Hill; and Sprung Enviroponics Ltd v Calgary (City) (1990), 103 A.R. 131. … 16 In my view, costs for past steps should be included in the security posted in this case. When the steps were taken, Old Manson Parties [the plaintiffs] had no reason to believe their ability to recover costs would be in jeopardy. Now, a concern has been raised, which New Crossroads [the defendant] has agreed justifies the posting of security. Where a party makes a transaction affecting its ability to answer for costs, it is just that the court require it to post the security necessary to restore the plaintiff to the position as to likelihood of recovering a possible costs order that it had before the transaction, as a condition of continuing its action. In Farley v. Alberta Hospital Assn. (1985), 60 A.R. 138, 1985 CarswellAlta 471 (Master), Master Funduk said, at p. 142: It should also be noted that in Watson the defendants total proposed costs were $3,085.00. The order which was upheld by the Court of Appeal required the plaintiff to give security in the sum of $3,000.00, even though the application was not made until after discoveries had been held. The order effectively ordered security for all the defendant's costs. It should be noted that in Crossman Beck, J., indicates it might not be appropriate to order security for past costs if the defendant was aware of the circumstances justifying his application for some time before the application. Lee J. disagreed, and at pp. 301-302 said: Irrespective of the American position, strict interpretation of the Alberta Rules of Court clearly show [sic] that “the Plaintiff” is liable for security for costs, not its solicitors (Rule 596). . . . . . The existence of contingency agreements in Alberta as a public policy matter essentially means that all counsel for all Plaintiffs in Alberta operating under a contingency agreement are seeking a share of any judgment, but do escape responsibility for any costs if they lose the case. This is simply not an unusual proposition given that contingency agreements are allowed in Alberta presently as sanctioned by Rules 615 and 616. The fact that the Plaintiff in this case resides outside of Alberta should not, in my view, subject her to any exceptional or extraordinary sanction as it relates to contingency agreements. Strictly speaking, there is no authority for the Defendant's proposition that the term “disbursements” includes payment of security for costs … My detailed review of the definition of the term “disbursement” leads me to believe that it does not include “security for costs”. 20. At that time the defendant company learned he had moved permanently out of Canada and back to the United States. Fixing the Amount and Experts' Fees Security for costs does not exceed party-and-party costs: Security for costs never exceeds (and may be less than) estimated party-and-party costs, which are rarely more than a fraction of solicitor-and-client costs on one side…Crothers v. Simpson Sears Ltd. (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. 1 (C.A.), at 11, per Côté J.A. On whether a security for costs order ought to anticipate that costs will ultimately be awarded as a multiple of one of the columns of Sched. C of the Rules of Court: Counsel for the defendant asks that the amount to be required as security for costs (apart from disbursements) should take into account the costs which would likely be awarded by the trial judge if the defendant were successful. He submits that in a case of this kind, involving a large amount of money, and complex issues of fact and law, there would “inevitably” be an award of costs on a multiple of Column 6 of Schedule C. Column 6 is the table of party-and-party costs to be awarded pursuant to rule 605(1) where the amount involved in the case is “over $150,000”, unless the trial judge orders that the amounts shall exceed the amounts set out in Column 6… I have given careful thought to whether the submission of counsel for the defendant should be accepted, that it is “inevitable” that the trial judge would order costs on triple Column 6, and that therefore the security required should reflect the result of such an order. No authority has been cited to me on the point. I recognize that the amount of security should cover the probable costs of the suit: Imperial Bank of China, India and Japan v. Bank of Hindustan, China and Japan (1866), 1 Ch. App. 437. But what are the “probable” costs? No doubt in the present case they would be at least in Column 6. But I hesitate to base my decision, as to the amount required to be furnished as security, upon what is at best an educated guess as to what the trial judge might or would order. Moreover, rule 605(1) states as a general rule that “the charges of barristers and solicitors … shall not exceed … Schedule C, depending upon the amount involved.” The provision at the beginning of rule 605(1)—“Unless otherwise ordered”—is an exception to the general rule. However common it may be to order a multiple of Column 6 in appropriate cases, it will be for the trial judge to decide whether this is an appropriate case, based upon the amount involved, the complexity and importance of the issues, and the length of the trial, and … any other factor which in the trial judge's opinion is relevant to the making of the order. I doubt that the submission that I should recognize what will be the “probable costs” of the suit is sufficient justification for assuming that the trial judge will or might exercise his or her discretion in a particular way. Security for costs for an action proceeding to trial should not include anticipated appeals from interlocutory orders: I do not think that when calculating the amount to be furnished as security for costs it is fair to impose upon the plaintiff the burden of securing the defendant's costs of appealing to the Court of Appeal from an interlocutory order made in this court. The luxury of taking an appeal is not a necessary step in proceeding to trial. Pocklington Foods Inc. v. Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R. 288 (Q.B.), at 294, per McDonald J. If one is claiming security for anticipated disbursements, it is necessary to provide evidentiary support for the claim. In a claim for security for disbursements, the applicant filed an affidavit which simply list “anticipated future costs” believed to be “reasonable estimates”. In denying the application, McDonald J. said: In my view it is inappropriate to make an order for security for such anticipated disbursements on the basis of such skeletal evidence. It may be that the defendant will incur such out-of-pocket expenses in order to prepare for trial. However, without being given details of such anticipated expenses, if I were to order security for these costs I would not be exercising my discretion judicially. The application for security for these costs is dismissed, with leave to renew the application upon more detailed evidence being placed before the court. Pocklington Foods Inc. v. Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R. 288 at 295 (Q.B.). And the Court of Appeal has said: No specific rule directs how to show the court what is a fit amount for security. The plaintiff would doubtless rely on the general rule that parties are to prove facts for chambers under oath, usually by affidavit. However, the question of amount is largely a matter of judgment or speculation about the future, plus the intentions of counsel. In most cases, requiring sworn evidence of such matters would do little good, and work much mischief. For example, counsel might have to swear the affidavits and so bar themselves from argument. Delicate issues of waiver of privilege would arise. In my view masters or judges should decide what evidence (if any) they need of amount, case by case, looking at what is practical and fair in each case. Often they will need no sworn evidence to show Sched. C items or fairly common disbursements, such as witness travel expenses. Had the defendants here asked for (say) $5,000 security for experts' fees, I doubt they would have needed any more evidence to support that than they gave. The chambers judge approached the question conscientiously, and made his own independent estimate, and halved the amounts sought for experts. But, awarding large sums such as $150,000 for experts' bills without significant evidence of amount makes me uneasy. Here the time and expense of investigating that amount further are justified. Therefore, I would leave in place the award of $89,022 for security for other costs, but would remit the $150,000 for security for experts. The Court of Queen's Bench should reassess that amount on further evidence as to amount. If any party wishes to have that amount set by a justice or master in chambers in the normal course, that will be done. I suggest that the parties might instead consider a consent order under RR. 418 ff. referring the amount to a specific clerk or deputy clerk with experience as a taxing officer, who is an official referee under R. 403. Then the judge would hear argument only if a party contested confirmation of the referee's report. Sprung Enviroponics Ltd. v. Calgary (City) (1990), 72 Alta. L.R. (2d) 237 at 246-47 (C.A.). In Ritter v. Hoag, 2003 ABQB 229, 2003 CarswellAlta 393, 334 A.R. 290, Burrows J., in discussing the calculation of security for costs, noted that the new “pay as you go rule” means that interlocutory application costs need not be considered when setting security for costs. At pp. 304-305, his Lordship said: Here the defendants have offered little evidence relevant to the determination of a quantum of security. They have observed that the proceedings to date have been expensive. There have been several applications for each of which written briefs have been prepared. There have been several days of cross-examination. More applications are likely before the matter goes to trial. The discovery process is likely to be time consuming. The claim being defended is for $40 million. I note the following statement in the newly published Stevenson and Côté, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, 2003 Juriliber, Vol 2, page 34-26: The court can only look at normal party-and-party costs when setting the amount of security, not extra costs on the possibility they would be awarded for failure to provide fraud. And ordinarily solicitor-client costs are not a proper basis for security. … Nor should the security include any costs for appeals or preparation or taxation of bills of costs. In my view it is also relevant to the determination of the quantum of security that the Rules and practice as to costs of interlocutory applications have changed in recent years. An order that costs arising from an interlocutory application will be determined at the end of the trial is no longer usual. The default now is that such costs should be awarded at the time the application is determined. A “pay as you go” approach is becoming common. It is supported by Rule 601(3) which provides that where no order as to costs is made, costs follow the event. To this point in this action, there have been few orders as to costs following applications. Rule 601(3) may not have been of significant assistance. The parties probably cannot agree as to which of them is entitled to costs. Applications to settle costs may be necessary. But if they are made and the costs are determined, the costs arising from past and future interlocutory applications need not be considered in determining the security. 22. McDonald agreed with Booth Construction in Pocklington Foods Inc. v. Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R. 288 (Q.B.). At p. 292, referring to Booth Construction, his Lordship said: Moreover, the plaintiff may not point to its claim as a “real” asset, and it should not be taken into account as if it were an asset, being an asset contingent upon the happening of a future event … The assets of the plaintiff must be real, substantial and exigible … In Laderoute v. Trader Publications (Alta), 2002 ABQB 467, 2002 CarswellAlta 596, 314 A.R. 306 (Master), Master Quinn said, at p. 307: I agree with what Master Breitkreuz said in Counter Inventory Services Ltd. v. King, [1985] A.J. No. 408 (Alta. Q.B. [In Chambers]), Action no. 8503 16662, namely: In my view Rule 595 would be meaningless if I were to adopt the plaintiff's argument. The discretionary aspect of the granting of the application may have much broader scope in all of the other categories listed in Rule 593(1) because none of the other categories have a limiting or qualifying provision equivalent to Rule 595. Therefore in order to give any meaning to Rule 595 it must mean that unless the plaintiff has sufficient property within the jurisdiction the order should be granted almost as a matter of right. The Court of Appeal has said: Rule 595 and many decided cases deny security if the plaintiff has sufficient exigible assets in Alberta, or if he brings any to, or creates any in, Alberta. See Seton's Forms of Judgments and Orders, 5th ed. (1891), vol. 1, p. 28; Chitty's Archbold, 14th ed. (1885), vol. 1, p. 397. Singh v. Dura (1988), Crothers v. Simpson Sears Ltd., 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 at 12 (C.A.). 23. Joint Assets Only consider the plaintiff's interest. First, it must be noted that the plaintiff and his wife are the joint owners of the land. The wife's interest in the land cannot be taken into consideration. What is left to consider is the plaintiff's one-half interest. Farley v. Alberta Hospital Assn. (1985), 60 A.R. 138 at 141 (Master). 24. Closely Held Private Corporation Look at the assets of both shareholders and creditors when considering what assets are available for security. In the case of a suit by a closely held private company, the enquiry about available security should go beyond the plaintiff, and should include the creditors or shareholders, or whoever else is pressing for and might benefit from the suit. Sylvester Import & Export Enterprises Ltd. v. Re/Max Real Estate Ltd. (1993), 135 A.R. 203 at 204 (C.A.). In Terra Energy Ltd. v. Kilborn Engineering Alberta Ltd. (1995), 168 A.R. 149 (Q.B.); [affirmed 169 A.R. 12], Mr. Justice Hart, in ordering security for costs, considered the principles applicable to an application for security for costs when the plaintiff is a closely held company. At pp. 156-57, his Lordship said: It is also well-established that where a plaintiff is a corporation, the court should not be unmindful of the potential for injustice to defendant where the corporation is a mere shell without financial substance… On the other hand it is equally clear that an order for security for costs should not be oppressive, such as to limit or restrict access to the court by a party who is unable to comply. As stated by Mr. Justice Reid of the Ontario High Court in the case of Wink (John) Ltd. v. Sico Inc. (1987), 57 O.R. (2d) 705 (H.C.) … There can be no question that an injustice would result if a meritorious claim were prevented from reaching trial because of the poverty of a plaintiff. If the consequences of an order for costs would be to destroy such a claim no order should be made. Injustice would be even more manifest if the impoverishment of the plaintiff were caused by the very acts of which plaintiff complains in the action. In the case before me I view the claim as being brought in substance and reality behind the corporate veil of the plaintiff by the 100 percent beneficial owner and sole director of the plaintiff company, Stephen Dunn. He's the real plaintiff. It is he who stands to win or lose depending upon the eventual outcome of the litigation. I find that the justice of the case requires that he stand responsible therefore, for taxable costs rather than shielding himself for this potential liability behind his wholly-owned limited liability company, the plaintiff … His Lordship then discussed Sylvester Import & Export Enterprises Ltd. v. Re/Max Real Estate Ltd. (1993), 135 A.R. 203 at 204 (C.A.), and concluded as follows, at p. 157: In Sylvester, two shareholders of the plaintiff company were ordered to give personal formal undertakings to the court to be personally responsible for any and all costs awarded against their company, and to secure this undertaking with a sum of cash to be paid in to court before further steps occurred in the action. I make a similar order here.
paragraphs.heading: Part 4. Managing Litigation

sentences.text: Commentary § 4.22:1 Rule 4.22 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Overview In Aski Construction Ltd. v.

Markos, 2017 ABCA 341, 2017 CarswellAlta 1845 Madam Justice Schutz gave this overview of the law relating to security for costs: 7 Security for costs is a discretionary order that balances the reasonable expectations and rights of the parties to come to a just and reasonable conclusion: Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367 at para 8.
A single appeal judge may award security for costs in accordance with Rules 14.67(1) and 4.22 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010.

Rule 4.22 states that the court may order a party to provide security for cost if the court considers it just and reasonable to do so, taking into account all of the following: a) whether it is likely the applicant for the order will be able to enforce an order or judgment against assets in Alberta; b) the ability of the respondent to the application to pay the costs award; c) the merits of the action in which the application is filed; d) whether an order to give security for payment of a costs award would unduly prejudice the respondent's ability to continue the action; e) any other matter the Court considers appropriate.
8 The onus is on the applicant to prove these factors weigh in their favour.

In previous decisions from this Court, concerns regarding a party's ability to pay costs coupled with modest prospects of an appeal's success have been sufficient to justify granting an application for security for costs: see for example Matty v Rammasoot, 2013 ABCA 170.
9 However, the analysis does not end there.

The Court has the discretion to refuse to order security for costs where the application has not been made promptly and there is a risk of resultant prejudice: Castillo v Go, 2002 ABCA 271 at paras 14, 18, 317 AR 195
Collins v Collins (Estate of), 2005 ABCA 41 at para 20.
This is particularly the case when delay in bringing the application for security for costs is unexplained: Marathon Canada Ltd v Enron Canada Corp, 2008 ABCA 424 at para 10, 446 AR 88.
In Parker v.
Parker, 2019 ABCA 114, 2019 CarswellAlta 574, 89 Alta.
L.R.

(6th) 104, Justice Greckol said: [4] A security for costs order is discretionary and balances the reasonable expectations of the parties with their rights in order to arrive at a just and reasonable outcome: Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367 (CanLII) at para 8.
The onus rests with the applicant to establish that the factors in r 4.22 are met: Aski Construction Ltd v Markos, 2017 ABCA 341 (CanLII) at para 8.

A failure to pay costs awarded in previous trial court processes, along with a demonstrated inability to pay costs if an appeal is unsuccessful, will be sufficient to grant a security for costs order in most cases: DataNet Information Systems, Inc v Belzil, 2011 ABCA 40 (CanLII)
(chambers) at para 4. “Access to justice does not equate to access to civil processes without fear of costs consequences”: ibid.
This statement was referred to with approval in Patton v.
Horse Racing Alberta, 2019 ABCA 182, 2019 CarswellAlta 928 at paragraph 11.
In Skolney v.
Nisha, 2018 ABCA 78, 2018 CarswellAlta 342, 10 R.F.L.
(8th) 34, Justice Greckol said: [21] Granting security for costs is a discretionary decision, which requires a judge to look to the equities of the case at bar before making an order.
Rule 4.22 states the Court “may” order security for costs if it “considers it just and reasonable to do so”. … That comment was also referred to with approval in Patton v.
Horse Racing Alberta, 2019 ABCA 182, 2019 CarswellAlta 928, at paragraph 13.
Also see the annotations under Rule 14.67.
Merits of the Action In Bechir v.
Gowling Lafleur Henderson LLP, 2017 ABQB 214, 2017 CarswellAlta 566, Justice Jeffrey discussed “merits of the action” as that term is used in R.
4.22(c): 12 As a general rule, the principles governing the consideration of Rule 4.22(c) are: … 2.
The court must attempt to look at the merits of the action, as difficult as that may be on an interlocutory application; 3.

The greater the likelihood of success for the plaintiff (if that can be reasonably assessed) the more the court should consider the potential unjustness of preventing a meritorious claim from proceeding; 4.

The converse is true: the smaller the likelihood of success for the plaintiff (if that can be reasonably assessed) the slower the court should be in denying security when security would otherwise be appropriate (1251165 Alberta Ltd v Wells Fargo Equipment Co, 2013 ABQB 533 at para 44) 13 For a security for cost application, the degree of rigour to the court's assessment of the merits under Rule 4.22(c) varies depending on how far into the litigation that the application for security for costs is brought: see PM&C Specialist Contractors Inc v Horton CBI Limited, 2015 ABQB 248 at para 15.
The later in the proceedings the application for security for costs is brought, the more in-depth the merits of the case will be examined.
Early in the proceedings, “it is difficult for any court … to weigh the merits.

It has heard no evidence and must attempt to rely on the submissions of counsel that arise from their pleadings and the questioning that has taken place to this point”: Provalcid Inc v Graff, 2014 ABQB 453 at para 97.

Therefore, if an application for security for costs is brought early in the proceedings, “it is neither possible, nor desirable, for the Court at this stage to determine which party's case is stronger”: Attila Dogan Construction v AMEC Americas Limited, 2011 ABQB 175 at para 17.
14 The consensus in the Alberta case law is that the merits of the case are relatively unimportant for applications brought early in the proceedings.
In Provalcid Inc, at para 97, Justice Yamauchi quoted with approval the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal decision in Wall v Horn Abbot Ltd

(2d) 96 at para 59: Second, while the merits of the plaintiff's case are relevant and may be considered, they should only be considered on the basis of undisputed facts, the pleadings, etc. and not on the basis of seriously disputed facts or assessments of credibility.
Third, consideration of the merits should only be decisive where they are clear and obvious.

In short, the law relating to consideration of the merits on interlocutory applications for security for costs is in harmony with the general reluctance to assess the merits of a claim or defence, other than in obvious cases, before trial.

[emphasis added] 15 Further, in Xpress Lube & Car Wash Ltd v Gill, 2011 ABQB 457 at para 11, Justice Hall stated that: In regard to Rule 4.22(c), the Court notes that neither action has proceeded through questioning.
Each action makes allegations which, if proven, could ground a judgment; that is to say, valid causes of action are alleged.
In these two cases it is simply too early for the Court to be persuaded that the actions do or do not have merit.
Therefore, nothing turns on this subrule at present.
Following the completion of questioning, this consideration may have greater weight.

[emphasis added] 16 In a recent decision, Alberta (Attorney General) v Alberta Power, 2017 ABQB 195 at para 26, Chief Justice Wittmann summarized the general principles applicable to the scope of a cross-examination on affidavit in Alberta.
The last of those is: 6.

The principle of proportionality is a consideration and undertakings otherwise answerable had the deponent had the information available at oral questioning ought to be answered provided the provision of the information would not be “overly onerous” and would likely significantly help the Court in the determination of the application: Dow Chemical Canada Inc[2008] A.J.
No.
1195 at para 5; Rozak Estate at para 41; PM&C Specialists Contractors at paras 9, 21.
17 While the merits of the case must be considered by the Court in a security for costs application under Rule 4.22(c), the Court does not attempt to determine which case is stronger.
Rather, if both parties establish a reasonably meritorious case on the pleadings and available evidence, Rule 4.22(c) should be a neutral consideration in the application.
The Rule Can Apply To A Defendant In Toronto Dominion Bank v.
Suitel Canada Executive Suites Corp., 2011 ABQB 519, 2011 CarswellAlta 2250, 527 A.R.

97, Justice Yamauchi said, at paragraphs 25-26: 25 At the outset, it should be noted that there is nothing preventing this Court from requiring Valerio, a defendant in this action, to post security for costs.
The opening words of Alberta Rules of Court r.
4.22, speak of “a party.” It is not limited to plaintiffs.
The wording in the Alberta Rules of Court that preceded the current rules, used the word “plaintiff” when it referred to a person against whom an order for security for costs could be sought.
The Alberta Legislature made an amendment to that rule to allow security for costs against “any party” where the court finds it just and reasonable to do so in the circumstances.
The Alberta Court of Appeal in Rushton v.
Condominium Plan No.
51 at 58, said that this amendment was enacted with the specific intent to make some defendants give security.

26 This Court must, however, exercise caution when it considers whether it should make such an award, as “no party should have to give security for costs as a condition of simply defending itself”: Toronto Dominion Bank v.
Szilagyi Farms Ltd.
No.
1223 at para.
21 (C.A.), citing Re Percy & Kelly Nickel, Cobalt, and Chrome Iron Mining Co.
D.
In 1400467 Alberta Ltd. v.
Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439, 2014 CarswellAlta 1208, 55 C.P.C.

(7th) 303, Madam Justice Veit said, at paragraphs 11–13: 11 Although Rule 4.22 clearly allows a court to order security for costs against a defendant, case law makes it clear that, even where a defendant fails to satisfy any of the specific factors mentioned in the rule, the issuance of such an order is far from automatic.

On the contrary, the general rule concerning the posting of security for costs by defendants is this: a plaintiff cannot call upon the defendant, even one resident out of the jurisdiction, to provide security for the plaintiff's costs.

12 The earliest explanation that I have been able to find of the policy underpinning this general rule in Canadian law was articulated in Lever: 8 The question is: Are there cases where the plaintiff “by law or practice” is entitled to obtain an order for security for costs?
The particular provisions of rule 5(1) deal with applications by defendants. … 12 Reference having been made to England and Ontario I have looked into the practice in those jurisdictions.
In England the general rule is stated by Jessel, M.R., in In re Percy and Kelly Nickel, Cobalt and Chrome Iron Mining Company, [1875-76] 2 Ch.D.

53]: The principle is well established that a person instituting legal proceedings in this country, and being abroad, so that no adverse order could be effectually made against him if unsuccessful, is by the rules of the court compelled to give security for costs.
That is perfectly well established and a perfectly reasonable principle; but it does not apply to a defendant or respondent who is brought here to defend himself.

If the person who institutes proceedings chooses to bring here people out of the jurisdiction, he must, in the first instance, consider whether or not it is worth his while to do so, even if he does not get costs.
He must take upon himself the risk of being unable to recover his costs, and cannot be allowed to say that the defendant whom he has chosen to bring here is not to defend himself.
13 In more recent days in England the principle remains the same.
It is said by Lord Greene, M.R., in Naamalooze v.
Bank of England, [1948] 1 All E.R.

468: That seems to me to be the right principle, that a defendant who is exercising the right of any defendant to defend himself against attack ought to be allowed to do so and not prevented or hampered by being ordered to give security.
14 In Ontario the same principle is adopted in Knickerbocker Trust Company of New York et al v.
Webster (1896), 17 P.R.
189, and Sample et al v.
McLaughlin et al (1897), 17 P.R.
Many more recent cases accept Knickerbocker as the authority for the general principle hereinbefore stated.
15 In my opinion, the practice, as in England, is and ought to be the practice and law in Nova Scotia.

16 It becomes clear that this is a case for application of the general principle that a plaintiff who is the real actor and initiator of the litigation cannot call upon the defendant, resident out of the jurisdiction, to provide security for the plaintiff's costs.
(Emphasis added) 13 So far as I am aware, the analysis set out in Lever has never been criticized or over-ridden in Canadian law.

Nor does the very general language of Rule 4.22, and of its immediate predecessor, create a dramatic departure from what has always been the approach of Canadian courts to security for costs; a revision to the Rules was necessary only in order to explicitly accommodate the relatively rare situations in which a plaintiff, or a defendant within the province, could properly be ordered to post security for costs.

Casual references to the general principle as set out in Lever are often made in contemporary decisions in Alberta and elsewhere: see, for example, by the Ontario Court of Appeal in Szylagyi Farms at para.
21, and by my colleague Yamauchi J. in Suitel Canada at para.

Indeed, the general rule is merely an application of common sense: a defendant has no choice about being a party to the litigation whereas a plaintiff typically has the choice, not only to commence litigation, but also, where to commence litigation.

In this case, the plaintiffs could have sued the defendants in Saskatchewan: the choice of law, and especially the choice of forum, contracts which the principal defendants executed and which made it obvious that Alberta was the forum conveniens were contracts that benefitted the plaintiffs and were therefore contracts the benefit of which the plaintiffs could have chosen to forego.
In every case, a prospective plaintiff who has a viable cause of action must make a decision about whether suing will throw good money after bad.
In some cases, a defendant must make an analogous choice: sometimes judgment will be conceded at an early stage merely so as not to incur further, larger, legal expenses which can never be recovered.
In other situations, a defendant allows judgment to go against it not because it does not have a defence, but because it doesn't have the finances to allow it to defend.
If a plaintiff doesn't think a defendant has exigible assets, its most obvious relief is not to sue that defendant.

It would clearly be unfair to grant a plaintiff security for costs when doing so will effectively give the plaintiff judgment but where the only negative thing against the defendant is that it is impecunious.
In HLFN Industry Relations Corporation v.

Horseman, 2019 ABQB 564, 2019 CarswellAlta 1533, Justice Ross said: [15] Generally, a plaintiff cannot call on defendants to post security for costs: 1400467 Alberta Ltd v Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439 (CanLII), at paras 11-12.

However, there is no bar for a plaintiff/defendant by counterclaim obtaining security for costs against defendants/plaintiffs by counterclaim on their counterclaim. “Defendants do not have to put up security to defend, but they may if they are advancing a counterclaim”: 1251165 Alberta Ltd v Wells Fargo Equipment Company Ltd, 2013 ABQB 533 (CanLII), at para 35 (“Wells Fargo”).

[16] The Court should follow a two-step process: first, considering the factors in Rule 4.22; and second, considering whether it is just and reasonable to grant security for costs: WestJet v ELS Marketing Inc, 2016 ABQB 172 (CanLII), paras 25-26.
In RDX Technologies Corporation v.

Appel, 2019 ABCA 338, 2019 CarswellAlta 1923, Justice Feehan said: [32] Orders for security for costs to be paid by defendants are unusual, particularly where the plaintiff has chosen to litigate in a jurisdiction where the defendants have no presence and have no choice in being parties to the action (see Jager Estate v Deadman, 2019 ABCA 99, paras 31-32; 1400467 Alberta Ltd v Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439, paras 11–13, 591 AR 40
Donaldson International Livestock Ltd v Znamensky Selekcionno-Gibridny Center LLC, 2010 ONCA 137, paras 13-14, 101 OR
(3d) 314, and Bouzari v Bahremani, 2014 ONCA 476, paras 7 and 15, 406 DLR

[33] On an application by a plaintiff, “even where a defendant fails to satisfy any of the specific factors mentioned in the rule, the issuance of … an order [for security for costs] is far from automatic.” On the contrary, the general rule is that a plaintiff cannot call upon a defendant, “even one resident out of the jurisdiction, to provide security for the plaintiff's costs” (Adderley, para 11) (see historically: In Re Percy and Kelly Nickel, Cobalt and Chrome Iron Mining Co, [1875-76] 2 Ch D 531
Naamalooze v Bank of England, [1948] 1 All ER 465 at p 468, Knickerbocker Trust Co of New York v Webster
(1896), 17 Ont PR 189 (CA); Sample v McLachlan
(1897), 17 Ont PR 490 (Div Ct); Lever v Harrietha

[34] A defendant “has no choice about being a party to the litigation whereas a plaintiff typically has the choice, not only to commence litigation, but also, where to commence litigation” (Adderley, para 13).
[35] These observations are particularly critical where there is a serious contest between the parties as to the appropriate forum for the litigation between them.
Onus Is First On Applicant; It Can Shift To Respondent In Toronto Dominion Bank v.
Suitel Canada Executive Suites Corp., 2011 ABQB 519, 2011 CarswellAlta 2250, 527 A.R.
97, the Plaintiff sought a security for costs order against a Defendant (Valerio).
A dispute arose as to the residence of Valerio.
Justice Yamauchi said, at paragraph 28: 28 There is contradictory evidence as to where Valerio resides.
The fact that he has a joint interest in the Condo belies an allegation that he is ordinarily resident in the Dominican Republic.
On the other hand, Valerio deposes that he and his spouse own a house in the Dominican Republic, which points to their residing in that country.
We must remember that TD Bank has the onus to make out its case under Alberta Rules of Court r.
4.22, before the burden shifts to Valerio: Hildebrandt v.
Fire on the Mountain Productions Inc., 2001 ABQB 301, 287 A.R.
363 at paras.
11 - 12 (Master).
Without more evidence, this Court cannot find that Valerio is a non-resident.
His Lordship then explained that once an applicant has satisfied its onus to bring itself within the Rule, the onus shifts to the respondent to show why an order ought not to be made.
At paragraph 31, Yamauchi, J. said: 31 TD Bank has satisfied the onus on it to bring itself within Alberta Rules of Court r.
Thus, the evidentiary burden shifts to Valerio to show that this Court should not post security for costs.
Why this shift?
Valerio is the only person who knows whether there is any reason why this Court should not order him to post security for costs: Besler at para.
15; Steffanson v.
Richardson Greenshields of Canada Ltd., [1992] A.J.
No.
In Mudrick Capital Management v.
Wright, 2018 ABQB 648, 2018 CarswellAlta 1855, 77 Alta.
L.R.
(6th) 421, Justice Yamauchi again discussed the onus of proof under both R.
4.22 and section 254 of the Business Corporations Act: [8] In Trimove Inc v Servus Credit Union, 2017 ABQB 50 (CanLII) at para 108, 44 CBR
(6th) 5, Nielsen J said the following: … Whether an application for security for costs is brought pursuant to s.
254 of the BCA or pursuant to Rule 4.22, the onus of proof does not change.
The applicant seeking security for costs bears the initial onus to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the respondent will be unable to pay its costs if the defence is successful.
If the applicant satisfies this onus, the evidentiary burden shifts to the respondent to show why the Court should not exercise its discretion to make such an Order against it.
[9] In the case at bar, the applicant Defendants bear the initial onus.

If the evidentiary burden shifts, the respondent Plaintiffs must establish why this Court should not exercise its discretion to make an order for security for costs, in the case of ABCA s 254 or whether it would be just and reasonable for this Court to grant an order for security for costs, in the case of Rules r 4.22.

In either case, the decision of whether to require the respondent to pay security for costs is discretionary: Amex Electrical Ltd v 726934 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 66 (CanLII) at paras 71-72, 582 AR 304, 99 Alta LR (5th) 1.
In Commercial Construction Supply Ltd. v.
Ghost Riders Farm Inc., 2016 ABQB 166, 2016 CarswellAlta 495, the defendants applied for an order requiring the plaintiff (CCS) to post security for costs.
Justice Nielsen said at paragraphs 22–25: 22 CCS is a body corporate and, as such, s.
254 of the BCA applies.
In all other cases not subject to other statutory enactments, Rule 4.22 applies.
Whether an application is brought pursuant to s.
254 of the BCA or pursuant to Rule 4.22, the onus of proof does not change.
The applicant seeking security for costs bears the initial onus to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the respondent will be unable to pay its costs if the defence is successful.

If the applicant satisfies this onus, the evidentiary burden shifts to the respondent to show why the Court should not exercise its discretion to make such an Order against it: Amex Electrical Ltd v 726934 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 66, 582 AR 304
Provalcid Inc v Graff, 2014 ABQB 453, 591 AR 117.
23 In Amex, Wakeling J.
(as he then was) set out two non-exhaustive lists of factors that might increase or decrease the likelihood that a court will award security for costs.

Factors favouring the granting of an Order for security for costs include (para 74): a) the respondent is a corporation and has no assets in Alberta; b) the respondent is a corporation and the assets it has in Alberta are of a nature or value that there is a substantial risk that the applicant may not be able to recover any costs award likely to be granted to it; c) the likelihood the respondent will receive judgment against the applicant is low; d) a security for costs Order will not prevent the respondent from prosecuting its action; e) the applicant is not seeking security for steps already taken; f) if the applicant has counterclaimed, and the issues raised by the counterclaim and the claim are different, this will not deter a court from granting security for costs; g) the applicant has applied for a security for costs Order at the earliest opportunity; and h) the resolution of the issues presented by the respondent's action is not important to the greater community.
24 Factors weighing against the granting of an Order for security for costs include (para 75):
(a) the applicant failed to apply for security for costs at the earliest opportunity
(b) the applicant seeks security for costs of steps already taken
(c) the respondent has assets in Alberta of a nature and value that there is little risk the applicant will be unable to recover any cost award likely to be granted to the applicant
(d) the likelihood the respondent will receive judgment against the applicant is high

(e) the shareholders of a corporation, which has no assets in Alberta or the assets it has in Alberta are of a nature and value that there is a substantial risk the applicant may not be able to recover any costs award likely to be granted to it, have assets in Alberta that would be sufficient to meet any costs award likely to be granted and have offered to provide personal guarantees
(f) a security for costs Order will prevent the respondent from prosecuting its action

(g) the applicant has counterclaimed and the issues raised by the counterclaim and the claim are the same or the counterclaim adds significantly to the action, with the potential to prolong discoveries and trial; and
(h) the resolution of the issue presented by the respondent's action is important to the community.
25 Yamauchi, J. in Provalcid commented on the foregoing factors and explained the interplay of s.
254 of the BCA and Rule 4.22: 92 It is worthwhile to note that many of the cases that Wakeling J cited for the propositions he put forth involve an interpretation of Rules r 4.22, or its predecessor.

There is logic to this approach inasmuch as the court, when considering whether the applicant has met the standard of proof required in BCA s 254, must consider the same factors when it is considering whether the applicant has met the standard of proof under Rules r 4.22, viz, those contained in Rules rr 4.22(a) through
The difference, however, is the ultimate determination the court must make when weighing those factors.

Under BCA s 254, the court must determine whether the body corporate is “unable to pay the costs of a successful defendant.” Under Rules r 4.22, the court must determine whether it is “just and reasonable” to require the respondent to provide security for costs.
93 Accordingly, it is appropriate for this Court to consider cases that were decided under Rules r 4.22, but only to determine whether [the applicant] has met his onus under BCA s 254.
In Conoco Phillips Canada Operations Ltd. v.

1835651 Alberta Ltd., 2020 ABQB 14, 2020 CarswellAlta 16 (Master), Master Robertson said: [80] Once again, I find myself in the position that there is conflicting case law from higher courts as to the burden, at least under rule 4.22, if not under section 254 as well.

[81] I conclude that under rule 4.22, which does not address the burden of proof, as long as there is a reasonable basis to show, or at least there is enough evidence to infer, that the respondent Alberta-based litigant has insufficient assets, the burden then shifts to the respondent to demonstrate that it does have sufficient assets. … 5.
Ability of the Respondent to Pay A Costs Award In Attila Dogan Construction v.
AMEC Americas Ltd., 2011 ABQB 175, 2011 CarswellAlta 407, 504 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 212, the defendant (AMEC) sought an order for security for costs against the Plaintiff in the amount of $11,030,302.
Chief Justice Wittmann considered the factors set out in R.

4.22, and, in relation to the factor of the ability of the respondent to pay a costs award, said, at paragraphs 12 and 13: 12 AD [the Plaintiff] has elected not to provide any evidence with regard to its ability to pay costs aside from pointing to the fact that it has been able to retain counsel in the jurisdiction and continues to operate a website.
Instead, it argues that, to the extent that it is unable to do so, its impecuniousity is related to the conduct of AMEC that is the subject of this action.
13 Retaining counsel and operating a website is not evidence that AD could satisfy an award of costs.
Nor is there any evidence to establish that any impecuniousity on AD's part has been caused by AMEC.
There is no evidence with respect to the financial condition of AD at all.

It seems to me that, where a plaintiff advances a claim of this magnitude, and does not dispute that it has no assets in this jurisdiction, that plaintiff risks having this factor weigh against it if it declines to bring any evidence with regard to its ability to satisfy an award of costs.
In Autoweld Systems Ltd. v.
CRC-Evans Pipeline International, Inc., 2011 ABQB 265, 2011 CarswellAlta 679, 504 A.R.
288; leave to appeal refused 2011 CarswellAlta 1355, 2011 ABCA 243, 515 A.R.
6, 57 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 429, the defendants brought an application for an order for security for costs against the plaintiff Autoweld Systems Ltd. in the sum of $605,975.
Justice McMahon reviewed the five factors set out in Rule 4.22.

In relation to the factor of “the ability of the Respondent to the application to pay the costs award”, his Lordship said, at paragraph 21: 21 … I need not determine that Autoweld “will be unable to pay the costs”.
The mandate is merely to consider the ability of Autoweld to pay in determining what is just and reasonable.
As I have described, the Plaintiff is not insolvent, nor is there evidence of outstanding judgments or significant debt and the Plaintiff seems to have a viable ongoing revenue generating business.
Nevertheless, the modest net assets of Autoweld suggests a real risk of an inability to pay substantial costs after protracted and expensive litigation.
What is a viable business today may not be so at the end of this litigation.
Alternatively, its revenue stream may be diverted elsewhere.

Interestingly, CRC-Evans cites a recent decision of the English Court of Appeal in which a security for costs order against Autoweld in certain unrelated English litigation was confirmed: Autoweld Systems Ltd. v.
Kito Enterprises LLC[2010] EWCA Civ.
