L.R.
(5th) 212, Chief Justice Wittmann had before him an application for an order requiring the Plaintiff (AD) to pay security for costs.

He set out a two step process which he followed in coming to his decision (at paragraphs 24 and 25): 24 Having carefully considered the factor in Rule 4.22 as discussed, I will approach the decision in two steps.
First, the factors considered in Rule 4.22(a–d) are weighted in favour of granting the application for security for costs.
A court may also take into account, pursuant to Rule 4.22(e), “any other matter the court considers appropriate”.

Particularly telling is AD's choice to tender absolutely no evidence on its behalf in opposition to the application, but rather to rely on the evidence put forward by AMEC, including AD's questioning of David Leonard on his affidavit.

The lack of any evidence put forward on behalf of AD, together with the fact that David Leonard's evidence was not significantly diluted or undermined by cross-examination, is, in my view a significant factor in favour of granting AMEC's application.

25 At the second step of the process, the court should ask itself whether it considers it just and reasonable to grant an application for security for payment of a costs award after it has taken into account all of the factors in Rule 4.22.
In this case, having considered all of the factors, I find it just and reasonable to grant AMEC's application and I will make an Order for security for payment of a costs award.
Quantum and Timing of Security for Costs In Attila Dogan Construction v.
AMEC Americas Ltd., 2011 ABQB 175, 2011 CarswellAlta 407, 504 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 212, the Defendant (AMEC) sought an order requiring the Plaintiff (AD) to pay security for costs in the amount of $11,030,302.
Wittmann, C.J. noted that “it is to be remembered that security for costs is security for party and party costs and not for legal fees.” (paragraph 26).
His Lordship awarded costs based on triple Column 5.
He said, at paragraph 27, “[i]t is appropriate, in circumstances where the claim is significant and the issues complex, to award security for costs on the basis of multiples of Column 5: Ritter v.
Hoag, 2003 ABQB 229, 2003 CarswellAlta 393, 334 A.R.
290; Tracer Industries[Tracer Industries Inc. v.
Shell Canada Ltd., 2004 ABQB 484].” Chief Justice Wittmann then discussed the timing of the payment of the security for costs.
At paragraphs 28–31, his Lordship said: 28 An award for security for costs is an exercise of the Court's discretion.
There is room within the scope of that discretion for a staged process, whereby security is posted at different points in the litigation: Law Society (Alberta) v.
Stinchcombe, 2009 ABQB 27, [2009] A.J.
No.
223; Western Canadian Shopping Centres Inc. v.
Dutton 2003 ABQB 376, 338 A.R.
Though the circumstances warrant an award for security for costs, to require AD to post $11 million at this stage of the litigation is, in my view, neither just nor reasonable.
However, it is just and reasonable at this time to order AD to post security for costs to the end of what is now referred to in the new Rules as questioning pursuant to Rule 5.17.
In the event that the estimate herein proves excessive or too little, it will remain open to the parties to bring the matter to me for a reassessment or adjustment as the litigation proceeds.

To be clear: at the conclusion of questioning, in the event that the estimate of costs herein was too high, AD will be entitled to a credit in respect of security for costs for the next stage of this litigation; in the event that my estimate was too low, this will be taken into account in determining the appropriate sum of security to be paid for the next stage.
29 AD is therefore ordered, within 35 days of this Order, to post security for costs on the basis of three times Column 5 through to the end of 80 days questioning.
Attached to David Leonard's affidavit is a draft Bill of Costs including taxable disbursements.
The expert witness fees claimed are $7 million.

In addition, the claim for the electronic database and full fees associated with maintaining and updating the same is $600,000, disbursement for the questioning reporter $82,425.00 (for 100 days), conduct money for discovery witnesses $60,000.

Other charges include the cost of transporting documents from the Middle East, London and Oakville to Calgary $20,000, long distance charges $3,500, facsimile charges $15,000, courier charges $20,000, photocopying charges $30,000.
My best estimate of disbursements that will be incurred until the end of questioning for discovery purposes, based on 80 days of questioning and the Bill of Costs presented is a further $800,000.
I am also aware that the GST is five percent.
30 Considering all of these factors, I am fixing the security for costs to be posted within thirty-five days of this Order at $1.6 million.

With respect to security for costs for expert reports, I am directing that when AMEC incurs a disbursement for an expert fee prior to the conclusion of questioning, upon proof of that disbursement or a certificate to that effect in a form satisfactory to the Court, the Court will consider adding security for costs for those expert fees.
I do not anticipate that that will necessarily occur before questioning is concluded, but if it does, the parties may approach me for an adjustment of the security before that time.
31 AMEC is given leave to apply for the next instalment of security for costs after questioning is completed.

AD may satisfy the requirement of security for costs to the end of questioning by paying $1,600,000 to the Clerk of the Court, or if agreed to by the parties in another form, such as a bond or irrevocable letter of credit.
If the parties cannot agree on the form of security, I will entertain a further application on this issue.
In Autoweld Systems Ltd. v.
CRC-Evans Pipeline International, Inc., 2011 ABQB 265, 2011 CarswellAlta 679, 504 A.R.
288; leave to appeal refused 2011 CarswellAlta 1355, 2011 ABCA 243, 515 A.R.
6, 57 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 429, Justice McMahon said, at paragraph 26: “…Security need not be ordered through to the end of trial.
Security can be amended as to the amount as the litigation proceeds.” In Emerex Oil and Gas Ltd. v.

Drover, 2016 ABQB 420, 2016 CarswellAlta 1485, Justice McCarthy confirmed that security for costs can be ordered on a solicitor-client basis: 89 Alberta courts have stated that security for costs can be awarded on a solicitor-client basis where it is likely that the costs will be awarded on a solicitor-client basis (Hamza v Hamza, 1997 ABCA 263 at para 17, 200 AR 342
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp v Canadian Commercial Bank, 1989 ABCA 150 at paras 24–26, 61 DLR
(4th) 161; Prairie Land Corp v Concert Properties Ltd, 2004 ABQB 726 at para 14, 364 AR 283).
Purpose of Rule The general purpose of the rule was stated by Andrekson J. as follows: In reviewing R.
593(1), it is clear that the rule was designed to protect the Defendant and to ensure that the Plaintiffs are able to answer the costs at the end of the proceedings.
Tkaczuk v.
Frocan (1993), 15 Alta.
L.R.
The security for costs rules are not designed to fund a lawsuit.
Nor can the Rules of Court relating to security for costs be combined with the prospective right to indemnity to obtain immediate funding.
Security for costs rules provide for security; they do not envisage funding in advance before the cause of action is decided.
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v.
Canadian Commercial Bank (1989), 68 Alta.
L.R.
Do Not Factor In Rules Regarding Double Costs In Home Exchange (Alberta) Ltd. v.
Goodyear Canada Inc., 2001 ABQB 673, 2001 CarswellAlta 1011, 291 A.R.

295, a defendant applied for security for costs in an amount that assumed that “Goodyear will beat a formal Offer of Judgment and thereby earn an entitlement to double costs.” In rejecting that approach, Lee J. said, at p.
300: … Taking Offers of Settlement into consideration would merely promote self-serving offers, thereby discouraging true settlement efforts.

For example, any Defendant could seek “double security” for costs on the basis that, if it is completely successful at trial, it will beat a nuisance value offer, and offers might be made for no other purpose than to escalate and double the claim for security for costs.
Further, the purpose of security for costs is financial in nature, that is, to protect a litigant's position with respect to costs.
The purpose of the double costs provisions in the Rules of Court is punitive in nature, that is, to promote settlement by imposing consequences for failing to settle.
It is not proper to import a punitive purpose into the security for costs provisions.
I further conclude that it is speculative to suggest at this stage that the Plaintiff will be punished by an award of costs, before the matter is even ready for trial.
When Security for Costs is Returnable in the Face of an Appeal In Polansky Electronics Ltd. v.
AGT Ltd., 2000 ABCA 46, 2000 CarswellAlta 109, 277 A.R.
55, 80 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 57, the plaintiff Polansky sued the defendant AGT for patent infringement.
The plaintiff was ordered to post, and did post, $75,000 as security for costs for the trial.
At trial the plaintiff was successful, and the defendant appealed.
The plaintiff sought the return of the $75,000 pending the appeal.

The Court of Appeal refused to order the return of the security for costs in the absence of evidence showing that the circumstances of the plaintiff had changed since the granting of the original order.
At p.

58, Russell J.A. said: The appeal is simply another step in the litigation process and it is possible that the Appellate court may making (sic) a ruling opposite to that of the trial judge with respect to the matter of costs.
The order for security of costs is prima facie evidence that when it was granted Polansky was in some respect financially insecure.

Thus, in the absence of evidence from Polansky showing a change in those circumstances, if money deposited for security for costs is returned, it can be inferred that there is still some risk that if the appeal is allowed the money will not be there to answer the purpose for which its payment was ordered.
Therefore, Polansky is not entitled to the return of the $75,000 at this time.
Delay in Bringing Application An application for security for costs must be made reasonably promptly: Wall v.
Wells, [1926] 37 B.C.R.
445 (C.A.); Shea's Hotel Sales Ltd. v.
Dell Hotel Ltd., supra; Whitfield v.
Thompson (1977), 3 B.C.L.R.
63 (S.C.); Allwise Const.
Ltd. v.
Tynan (1977), 5 B.C.L.R.
Ct.); Frank Hillis Logging Co. v.
Hoeya Sound Logging Ltd., [1971] 2 W.W.R.
Failure to do so is not necessarily fatal to the application.

If a plaintiff is lulled into the false belief that he may proceed with the action without being called upon to advance security and does act upon that belief, a subsequent application for security will not be allowed, at least as to past costs.
Before such delay doctrine can be applied, there must be some indication that the delay has had the effect of leading the plaintiff into a false sense of security or has worked to his prejudice.
United Paint & Coating Canada Ltd. v.
St.
Laurent (1980), 13 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 134 (Master), at 140, per Master Funduk.

And McDonald J. has said: Even if there has been some delay on the part of the defendant in the present case, the order should be granted unless the plaintiff shows that it suffered some prejudice from the delay or was induced into believing that it was safe in incurring costs without risking facing an order for security for costs.
In Officine Vittorio Ceccoli, S.P.A. v.
British Columbia Hydro & Power Authority, [1971] 3 W.W.R.
C.A.), Bull, J.A., said at p.
83: In the absence of any time limitation imposed by rule, delay of itself is not in my opinion a valid answer to the motion.

It has been held many times that applications for security for costs must be brought promptly but the reason for this is, I think, that delay may induce the belief in a plaintiff that he may be reasonably safe incurring costs on his own behalf without the risk of being confronted with an order for security with which he may be unable to comply and thus be compelled to throw away the expense theretofore incurred in the prosecution of his case.
Pocklington Foods Inc. v.
Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R.
Costs Already Incurred In Manson Insulation Products Ltd. v.
Crossroads C&I Distributors, 2014 ABQB 634, 2014 CarswellAlta 1892, Mr.
Justice Poelman addressed the question of whether security for costs orders should encompass costs for steps taken before the application is made.

At paragraphs 13 and 16, his Lordship said: 13 New Crossroads [the defendant] relies on Amex Electrical Ltd v 726934 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 66, for the proposition that security for costs should be prospective only, limited to costs for steps not yet taken: Amex, paras 74(e) and 75(b).
With respect, in my view that proposition is not sound.
Amex cites many authorities in support, but not Beacon Hill Service (2000) Ltd v Esso Petroleum Canada, 2000 ABCA 326, 281 A.R.
The point was squarely before the court in that case, because the case management judge had included costs for steps already taken when the order was made.
For the court, Picard JA held that “a judge is not precluded from looking at past costs along with future ones in setting the quantum”: para 10.
Determining the amount is highly discretionary, and must be done on a case by case basis: Beacon Hill; and Sprung Enviroponics Ltd v Calgary (City) (1990), 103 A.R.
131. … 16 In my view, costs for past steps should be included in the security posted in this case.
When the steps were taken, Old Manson Parties [the plaintiffs] had no reason to believe their ability to recover costs would be in jeopardy.
Now, a concern has been raised, which New Crossroads [the defendant] has agreed justifies the posting of security.

Where a party makes a transaction affecting its ability to answer for costs, it is just that the court require it to post the security necessary to restore the plaintiff to the position as to likelihood of recovering a possible costs order that it had before the transaction, as a condition of continuing its action.
In Farley v.
Alberta Hospital Assn.
138, 1985 CarswellAlta 471 (Master), Master Funduk said, at p.
142: It should also be noted that in Watson the defendants total proposed costs were $3,085.00.
The order which was upheld by the Court of Appeal required the plaintiff to give security in the sum of $3,000.00, even though the application was not made until after discoveries had been held.
The order effectively ordered security for all the defendant's costs.

It should be noted that in Crossman Beck, J., indicates it might not be appropriate to order security for past costs if the defendant was aware of the circumstances justifying his application for some time before the application.
A delay in making the application after the defendant becomes aware of the circumstances may weigh against the defendant in ordering security for costs already incurred.
Contingency Fee Arrangements In Jorgensen v.
San Francisco Gifts Ltd.
L.R.

(3d) 288 (Q.B.), it was argued that since the plaintiff's lawyer, under a contingency fee agreement, had agreed to finance the disbursements of the plaintiff, then the lawyer should be liable to post security for costs.
American authority was relied upon.
Lee J. disagreed, and at pp.

301-302 said: Irrespective of the American position, strict interpretation of the Alberta Rules of Court clearly show [sic] that “the Plaintiff” is liable for security for costs, not its solicitors (Rule 596). . . . . .

The existence of contingency agreements in Alberta as a public policy matter essentially means that all counsel for all Plaintiffs in Alberta operating under a contingency agreement are seeking a share of any judgment, but do escape responsibility for any costs if they lose the case.
This is simply not an unusual proposition given that contingency agreements are allowed in Alberta presently as sanctioned by Rules 615 and 616.
The fact that the Plaintiff in this case resides outside of Alberta should not, in my view, subject her to any exceptional or extraordinary sanction as it relates to contingency agreements.

Strictly speaking, there is no authority for the Defendant's proposition that the term “disbursements” includes payment of security for costs … My detailed review of the definition of the term “disbursement” leads me to believe that it does not include “security for costs”.
Where Plaintiff Subsequently Leaves The plaintiff leaving Alberta after commencement of the action may lead to security for costs.
The plaintiff was examined for discovery on March 1, 1991.
At that time the defendant company learned he had moved permanently out of Canada and back to the United States.
At the time the present action was commenced the plaintiff was still residing in Edmonton.
Where a plaintiff goes to reside permanently abroad after the institution of a suit security for costs may be ordered: Aldridge v.
Dogwood Sales Agencies Ltd.
Pugh v.
Biomira Inc.
380 (Master), at 381, per Master Quinn.

Fixing the Amount and Experts' Fees Security for costs does not exceed party-and-party costs: Security for costs never exceeds (and may be less than) estimated party-and-party costs, which are rarely more than a fraction of solicitor-and-client costs on one side…Crothers v.
Simpson Sears Ltd.
L.R.
1 (C.A.), at 11, per Côté J.A.
On whether a security for costs order ought to anticipate that costs will ultimately be awarded as a multiple of one of the columns of Sched.

C of the Rules of Court: Counsel for the defendant asks that the amount to be required as security for costs (apart from disbursements) should take into account the costs which would likely be awarded by the trial judge if the defendant were successful.
He submits that in a case of this kind, involving a large amount of money, and complex issues of fact and law, there would “inevitably” be an award of costs on a multiple of Column 6 of Schedule C.

Column 6 is the table of party-and-party costs to be awarded pursuant to rule 605(1) where the amount involved in the case is “over $150,000”, unless the trial judge orders that the amounts shall exceed the amounts set out in Column 6… I have given careful thought to whether the submission of counsel for the defendant should be accepted, that it is “inevitable” that the trial judge would order costs on triple Column 6, and that therefore the security required should reflect the result of such an order.
No authority has been cited to me on the point.
I recognize that the amount of security should cover the probable costs of the suit: Imperial Bank of China, India and Japan v.
Bank of Hindustan, China and Japan (1866), 1 Ch.
App.
But what are the “probable” costs?
No doubt in the present case they would be at least in Column 6.
But I hesitate to base my decision, as to the amount required to be furnished as security, upon what is at best an educated guess as to what the trial judge might or would order.

Moreover, rule 605(1) states as a general rule that “the charges of barristers and solicitors … shall not exceed … Schedule C, depending upon the amount involved.” The provision at the beginning of rule 605(1)—“Unless otherwise ordered”—is an exception to the general rule.

However common it may be to order a multiple of Column 6 in appropriate cases, it will be for the trial judge to decide whether this is an appropriate case, based upon the amount involved, the complexity and importance of the issues, and the length of the trial, and … any other factor which in the trial judge's opinion is relevant to the making of the order.

I doubt that the submission that I should recognize what will be the “probable costs” of the suit is sufficient justification for assuming that the trial judge will or might exercise his or her discretion in a particular way.
Pocklington Foods Inc. v.
Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R.
288 (Q.B.), at 293-95, per McDonald J.

Security for costs for an action proceeding to trial should not include anticipated appeals from interlocutory orders: I do not think that when calculating the amount to be furnished as security for costs it is fair to impose upon the plaintiff the burden of securing the defendant's costs of appealing to the Court of Appeal from an interlocutory order made in this court.
The luxury of taking an appeal is not a necessary step in proceeding to trial.
Pocklington Foods Inc. v.
Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R.
288 (Q.B.), at 294, per McDonald J.
If one is claiming security for anticipated disbursements, it is necessary to provide evidentiary support for the claim.
In a claim for security for disbursements, the applicant filed an affidavit which simply list “anticipated future costs” believed to be “reasonable estimates”.
In denying the application, McDonald J. said: In my view it is inappropriate to make an order for security for such anticipated disbursements on the basis of such skeletal evidence.
It may be that the defendant will incur such out-of-pocket expenses in order to prepare for trial.
However, without being given details of such anticipated expenses, if I were to order security for these costs I would not be exercising my discretion judicially.
The application for security for these costs is dismissed, with leave to renew the application upon more detailed evidence being placed before the court.
Pocklington Foods Inc. v.
Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R.
And the Court of Appeal has said: No specific rule directs how to show the court what is a fit amount for security.
The plaintiff would doubtless rely on the general rule that parties are to prove facts for chambers under oath, usually by affidavit.
However, the question of amount is largely a matter of judgment or speculation about the future, plus the intentions of counsel.
In most cases, requiring sworn evidence of such matters would do little good, and work much mischief.
For example, counsel might have to swear the affidavits and so bar themselves from argument.
Delicate issues of waiver of privilege would arise.
In my view masters or judges should decide what evidence (if any) they need of amount, case by case, looking at what is practical and fair in each case.
Often they will need no sworn evidence to show Sched.
C items or fairly common disbursements, such as witness travel expenses.
Had the defendants here asked for (say) $5,000 security for experts' fees, I doubt they would have needed any more evidence to support that than they gave.
The chambers judge approached the question conscientiously, and made his own independent estimate, and halved the amounts sought for experts.
But, awarding large sums such as $150,000 for experts' bills without significant evidence of amount makes me uneasy.
Here the time and expense of investigating that amount further are justified.
Therefore, I would leave in place the award of $89,022 for security for other costs, but would remit the $150,000 for security for experts.
The Court of Queen's Bench should reassess that amount on further evidence as to amount.
If any party wishes to have that amount set by a justice or master in chambers in the normal course, that will be done.
I suggest that the parties might instead consider a consent order under RR.
418 ff. referring the amount to a specific clerk or deputy clerk with experience as a taxing officer, who is an official referee under R.
Then the judge would hear argument only if a party contested confirmation of the referee's report.
Sprung Enviroponics Ltd. v.
Calgary (City) (1990), 72 Alta.
L.R.
In Ritter v.
Hoag, 2003 ABQB 229, 2003 CarswellAlta 393, 334 A.R.

290, Burrows J., in discussing the calculation of security for costs, noted that the new “pay as you go rule” means that interlocutory application costs need not be considered when setting security for costs.
At pp.
304-305, his Lordship said: Here the defendants have offered little evidence relevant to the determination of a quantum of security.
They have observed that the proceedings to date have been expensive.
There have been several applications for each of which written briefs have been prepared.
There have been several days of cross-examination.
More applications are likely before the matter goes to trial.
The discovery process is likely to be time consuming.
The claim being defended is for $40 million.

I note the following statement in the newly published Stevenson and Côté, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, 2003 Juriliber, Vol 2, page 34-26: The court can only look at normal party-and-party costs when setting the amount of security, not extra costs on the possibility they would be awarded for failure to provide fraud.
And ordinarily solicitor-client costs are not a proper basis for security. … Nor should the security include any costs for appeals or preparation or taxation of bills of costs.
In my view it is also relevant to the determination of the quantum of security that the Rules and practice as to costs of interlocutory applications have changed in recent years.
An order that costs arising from an interlocutory application will be determined at the end of the trial is no longer usual.
The default now is that such costs should be awarded at the time the application is determined.
A “pay as you go” approach is becoming common.
It is supported by Rule 601(3) which provides that where no order as to costs is made, costs follow the event.
To this point in this action, there have been few orders as to costs following applications.
Rule 601(3) may not have been of significant assistance.
The parties probably cannot agree as to which of them is entitled to costs.
Applications to settle costs may be necessary.
But if they are made and the costs are determined, the costs arising from past and future interlocutory applications need not be considered in determining the security.
Assets Must Be Real, Substantial and Exigible Any assets of Booth must, in my view, be not only real and substantial but also exigible.
In Rundle Maintenance Ltd. v.
Stevens (1977), 4 A.R.
321 (Dist.
Ct.), Stevenson D.C.J.
(as he then was) stated at p.
324: The existence of some assets which might be available to answer the defendant's claim does not satisfy the Rule 595.
The assets in question must be exigible and substantial.

In Shea's Hotel it was stated that the claim against a defendant may be substantial but it is not a real asset and should not be taken into account, i.e., the assets of a plaintiff should not be calculated by including an asset contingent upon the happening of a future event.
Booth Construction Ltd. v.
Estabrook Construction Ltd.
L.R.
(2d) 157 (Q.B.), at 163, per Egbert J.
Mr.
Justice D.C.
McDonald agreed with Booth Construction in Pocklington Foods Inc. v.
Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) (1994), 153 A.R.
At p.

292, referring to Booth Construction, his Lordship said: Moreover, the plaintiff may not point to its claim as a “real” asset, and it should not be taken into account as if it were an asset, being an asset contingent upon the happening of a future event … The assets of the plaintiff must be real, substantial and exigible … In Laderoute v.
Trader Publications (Alta), 2002 ABQB 467, 2002 CarswellAlta 596, 314 A.R.
306 (Master), Master Quinn said, at p.
307: I agree with what Master Breitkreuz said in Counter Inventory Services Ltd. v.
King, [1985] A.J.
No.
408 (Alta.
Q.B.
[In Chambers]), Action no.
8503 16662, namely: In my view Rule 595 would be meaningless if I were to adopt the plaintiff's argument.

The discretionary aspect of the granting of the application may have much broader scope in all of the other categories listed in Rule 593(1) because none of the other categories have a limiting or qualifying provision equivalent to Rule 595.
Therefore in order to give any meaning to Rule 595 it must mean that unless the plaintiff has sufficient property within the jurisdiction the order should be granted almost as a matter of right.
The Court of Appeal has said: Rule 595 and many decided cases deny security if the plaintiff has sufficient exigible assets in Alberta, or if he brings any to, or creates any in, Alberta.
See Seton's Forms of Judgments and Orders, 5th ed.
28; Chitty's Archbold, 14th ed.
Singh v.
Dura (1988), Crothers v.
Simpson Sears Ltd., 59 Alta.
L.R.
Joint Assets Only consider the plaintiff's interest.
First, it must be noted that the plaintiff and his wife are the joint owners of the land.
The wife's interest in the land cannot be taken into consideration.
What is left to consider is the plaintiff's one-half interest.
Farley v.
Alberta Hospital Assn.
138 at 141 (Master).
Closely Held Private Corporation Look at the assets of both shareholders and creditors when considering what assets are available for security.

In the case of a suit by a closely held private company, the enquiry about available security should go beyond the plaintiff, and should include the creditors or shareholders, or whoever else is pressing for and might benefit from the suit.
Sylvester Import & Export Enterprises Ltd. v.
Re/Max Real Estate Ltd.
In Terra Energy Ltd. v.
Kilborn Engineering Alberta Ltd.
149 (Q.B.); [affirmed 169 A.R.
Justice Hart, in ordering security for costs, considered the principles applicable to an application for security for costs when the plaintiff is a closely held company.
At pp.

156-57, his Lordship said: It is also well-established that where a plaintiff is a corporation, the court should not be unmindful of the potential for injustice to defendant where the corporation is a mere shell without financial substance… On the other hand it is equally clear that an order for security for costs should not be oppressive, such as to limit or restrict access to the court by a party who is unable to comply.
As stated by Mr.
Justice Reid of the Ontario High Court in the case of Wink (John) Ltd. v.
Sico Inc.
(2d) 705 (H.C.) … There can be no question that an injustice would result if a meritorious claim were prevented from reaching trial because of the poverty of a plaintiff.
If the consequences of an order for costs would be to destroy such a claim no order should be made.
Injustice would be even more manifest if the impoverishment of the plaintiff were caused by the very acts of which plaintiff complains in the action.

In the case before me I view the claim as being brought in substance and reality behind the corporate veil of the plaintiff by the 100 percent beneficial owner and sole director of the plaintiff company, Stephen Dunn.
He's the real plaintiff.
It is he who stands to win or lose depending upon the eventual outcome of the litigation.

I find that the justice of the case requires that he stand responsible therefore, for taxable costs rather than shielding himself for this potential liability behind his wholly-owned limited liability company, the plaintiff … His Lordship then discussed Sylvester Import & Export Enterprises Ltd. v.
Re/Max Real Estate Ltd.
203 at 204 (C.A.), and concluded as follows, at p.

157: In Sylvester, two shareholders of the plaintiff company were ordered to give personal formal undertakings to the court to be personally responsible for any and all costs awarded against their company, and to secure this undertaking with a sum of cash to be paid in to court before further steps occurred in the action.
I make a similar order here.
